snippets.name: Controlled update flow (download / verify / apply)
snippets.code:
# 1. Stage without finalizing on the next reboot
bootc upgrade --download-only

# 2. Inspect
bootc status --verbose            # human: "Download-only: yes"
bootc status --format=json | jq '{
  staged_digest:  .status.staged.image.imageDigest,
  download_only:  .status.staged.downloadOnly,
  booted_digest:  .status.booted.image.imageDigest,
  rollback_digest:.status.rollback.image.imageDigest
}'

# 3a. Apply exactly what was downloaded (no registry round-trip), reboot now
bootc upgrade --from-downloaded --apply
# 3b. ...or unlock it for the next natural reboot
bootc upgrade --from-downloaded

# Emergency: swap boot order back. Discards any staged upgrade.
# /etc changes made since the previous deployment are LOST.
bootc rollback --apply

gotchas: The digest path is triple-nested for the ref but NOT for the digest: `.status.booted.image.imageDigest` (digest) vs `.status.booted.image.image.image` (ref string). BootEntry.image is an ImageStatus; ImageStatus.image is an ImageReference; ImageReference.image is the string. Getting this wrong is the most likely CI bug.
`bootc status --booted` omits `.status.staged` and `.status.rollback` content you may want. Use plain `bootc status --format=json` when you need staged/rollback in the same call.

A restrictive policy.json alone does NOT enforce signatures. The deployment must also carry sigverify=ContainerPolicy, set via `--enforce-container-sigpolicy` at install or switch. Default is ContainerPolicyAllowInsecure, which defers to policy.json's default — and the shipped default is `insecureAcceptAnything`. Gate CI on `.status.booted.image.image.signature == "containerPolicy"`, not on the presence of a policy file.

`use-sigstore-attachments: true` in /etc/containers/registries.d/*.yaml is REQUIRED for cosign signatures. Built-in default is to not read attachments at all, so verification silently cannot find the signature. Also: one scope may appear in at most one registries.d file — conflicting or split configs are an error.

cosign signatures bind only a repository, so signedIdentity must be matchRepository/exactRepository, and upstream explicitly warns this does not stop substituting a signed image under a different tag. Pin by digest if that matters.

Only ONE rollback deployment exists. libostree's default garbage-collects everything except the merge and booted deployments, and bootc's staged finalization passes no RETAIN flags. You cannot roll back two versions unless you `ostree admin pin` a deployment yourself.

`bootc rollback` discards a staged upgrade, and reverts /etc to the previous deployment's state. Any post-deploy /etc writes (enrollment, certs, tuned configs) vanish. Also, an active `bootc-fetch-apply-updates.timer` can immediately undo your rollback — upstream says to use rollback only with an agent in active control.

greenboot is NOT preinstalled on Fedora bootc standard/minimal/minimal-plus, nor on Universal Blue's ublue-os/main base. Only the Fedora bootc IoT variant ships it. Plan to `dnf install -y greenboot greenboot-default-health-checks` in the Containerfile.

The shell greenboot is deprecated; RPM >= 0.16.0 is greenboot-rs, which ships only greenboot-healthcheck.service, greenboot-set-rollback-trigger.service and greenboot-success.target. Blog-post commands like `systemctl enable greenboot-grub2-set-counter greenboot-grub2-set-success redboot-auto-reboot ...` will fail on current images.

greenboot's rollback depends on the GRUB boot_counter: the 08_greenboot.cfg is installed under /usr/lib/bootupd/grub2-static/configs.d/, i.e. it needs bootupd static GRUB configs. If boot_counter is never set, greenboot logs RED and bails with "manual intervention required" without rolling back. bootc's composefs/UKI backend does not configure boot entry counting at all today — you lose automatic rollback there.
greenboot's RPM still carries `Requires: rpm-ostree` even in the bootc-oriented greenboot-rs, so you pull rpm-ostree into the image whether you use it or not.

bootc-image-builder's `--type` cannot take a comma- or space-separated list; repeat the flag. And `--type iso` / `anaconda-iso` / `bootc-installer` are three different things — `bootc-installer` requires a container with Anaconda inside plus `--bootc-installer-payload-ref`.

In an ISO build, a `[customizations.installer.kickstart]` block is not supported alongside `[[customizations.user]]`. Do all user setup inside the kickstart. bootc-image-builder adds the `ostreecontainer` line and nothing else — no partitioning, network or lang defaults.

Fedora bootc images have no default rootfs type configured, so `--rootfs` is mandatory for them; the CentOS stream9 example omits it because that image sets one. With `--rootfs btrfs` you lose all custom /var mountpoints.
The root filesystem's final size is max(configured minsize, 2x base container size), so a `minsize = "10 GiB"` can silently come out larger. Don't assert exact partition sizes.

bootc has no `--tls-verify` flag (use registries.conf.d `insecure=true`), and its registry credentials come from /etc/ostree/auth.json, not the usual containers auth path. `podman pull` working is not evidence that `bootc upgrade` will.

`bootc container lint` has only exit 0 / exit 1. A fatal lint and an internal crash both exit 1; the only discriminator is the literal `Checks failed: N` on stderr. `--list` emits YAML but upstream explicitly forbids parsing it.

bootc's staged deployments are finalized at SHUTDOWN, so a finalization failure is discovered on the *next* boot via ostree-boot-complete.service. Check `journalctl -u ostree-finalize-staged.service -b -1`, not `-b`.
If you pin images by digest, `bootc upgrade` becomes a permanent no-op and every update must be a `bootc switch`. Any timer-based auto-update will look like it's working while doing nothing.
blockers: The osbuild/bootc-image-builder GitHub repo is ARCHIVED — it has been merged into osbuild/image-builder (now at osbuild/image-builder/bootc-image-builder/). The README content and the podman invocation are byte-identical in the new location and the published container image quay.io/centos-bootc/bootc-image-builder:latest is still what upstream documents, so nothing is broken today. But issue links, PRs and any CI pinning the old repo need repointing, and long-term the two projects are stated to be converging ('Both projects are very close... We expect eventual merger').

The premise URL bootc-dev.github.io/bootc/ 301-redirects to bootc.dev/bootc/. Not fatal, but any CI job or doc-link checker hitting the github.io host will take a redirect. The GitHub org/repo bootc-dev/bootc is correct and live; note the older containers/bootc path also still appears in upstream READMEs.

There is no way to retain more than one rollback deployment through normal bootc operation. If the plan assumes 'roll back to any of the last N images', that is false: default retention is booted + one rollback, and the only escape hatch is manually running `ostree admin pin` (which bootc does not expose as a verb, though the resulting pinned entries do show up in .status.otherDeployments with pinned: true).

The premise that greenboot ships on Universal Blue / Fedora bootc images is wrong for the images most people mean. Verified absent from Fedora bootc standard/minimal/minimal-plus manifests and from ublue-os/main, ublue-os/bluefin and ublue-os/aurora. Present only in the Fedora bootc IoT manifest (and ublue-os/bazzite carries a greenboot.conf override, implying it arrives there some other way). Any plan that assumes health-check rollback is on by default needs an explicit install step.

If the target is the composefs/UKI backend rather than the default ostree backend, automatic greenboot rollback does not work: upstream states the composefs backend does not configure boot loader entry counting yet and has no bootc-boot-complete.service equivalent. Health-check-driven rollback is only available on the ostree + GRUB/bootupd path today.

area: Making package removal real in an OCI bootc image: (A) hhd-dev/rechunk, (B) removing packages / a whole DE from a Fedora bootc base, (C) measuring bytes saved. Researched 2026-09-20.

facts.claim: hhd-dev/rechunk's GitHub Action has NO `rawhide` input. The complete input list in action.yml is: ref (required), prev-ref, clear-plan, prev-ref-fail, max-layers, skip_compression, labels, description, version (default `<date>`), pretty, rechunk (default `ghcr.io/hhd-dev/rechunk:latest`), keep-ref, changelog, git, revision, formatters, meta. Outputs: ref, version, location, changelog, manifest.
facts.evidence: gh api repos/hhd-dev/rechunk/contents/action.yml (read in full, master branch). Also `gh api -X GET search/code -f q="rawhide repo:hhd-dev/rechunk"` => total_count 0, and grep for rawhide/RAWHIDE in 3_chunk.sh, src/rechunk/__main__.py, fedora.py, utils.py returns nothing.
facts.impact: Drop `rawhide:` from any planned step — it would be silently ignored by GitHub Actions composite inputs, or fail input validation. If you wanted rawhide-specific behavior, it has to come from your own matrix/env, not from rechunk.

facts.claim: rechunk REQUIRES rootful (not rootless) podman and specifically the `ubuntu-24.04` runner, not `ubuntu-latest`. Every podman call in the composite action is literally `sudo podman ...` and `-u 0:0`.
facts.evidence: readme.md: "The action in this repository uses advanced podman features (e.g., mount) and requires both root access (**not rootless** execution) and the **Ubuntu 24.04** runner (not **latest** as of this writing). It is recommended to build your image with buildah or podman using root (e.g., `sudo podman build`) so that it can be mounted directly by this action". action.yml steps use `sudo podman create`, `sudo podman mount`, `sudo podman run --rm ... -u 0:0`. The repo's own .github/workflows/online_test_deck.yml uses `runs-on: ubuntu-24.04`.
facts.impact: Your build job must be `runs-on: ubuntu-24.04` and must build the image with `sudo podman build` (rootful storage), otherwise `podman create <ref>` inside the action cannot find the image.

facts.claim: rechunk adds ~6-10 minutes of wall clock: ~2 min preparing the image for committing, ~3 min for ostree to create the commit, ~4 min for ostree-rs-ext to produce the gzipped OCI dir. `skip_compression: true` saves 3-5 min / ~30% of runtime and is only safe if you recompress on upload (e.g. zstd:chunked).
facts.evidence: readme.md "### Time cost" section, verbatim: "`Rechunk` adds around 6-10 minutes of processing time to producing an OCI image. Around 2 of those minutes are spent preparing the image for committing, 3 minutes for `ostree` creating the commit, and 4 minutes (can be lowered by skipping gzip compression) for `ostree-rs-ext` to produce the final gziped oci directory." action.yml input `skip_compression`: "Skip compression of the output image. Use only if you are recompressing the output (e.g., zstd:chunked). Saves 3-5min or 30% of runtime."
facts.impact: Budget +10 min per build. Set skip_compression only if you push with `skopeo copy --compression-format zstd:chunked` or similar; otherwise you ship uncompressed-ish layers.

facts.claim: rechunk DESTROYS layer inheritance from the base image. It mounts the image, deletes /sysroot's ostree repo, commits the flattened tree as a fresh OSTree commit, and re-encapsulates into N brand-new layers. The output shares no layers with the parent base image. This is exactly why deletions become real bytes saved.
facts.evidence: readme.md: "It flattens the file system tree, thereby removing files that were replaced in later OCI layers, then re-partitions the image into a set of N equally sized layers." and "Drops unused files and lowers image size - E.g., if you extend Kinoite and replace the kernel, you do not have to ship the old kernel which was part of the original OSTree commit." Same property confirmed for the chunkah path in ublue-os/image-template Justfile: "You may run into space issues on github runners as we are making a complete copy of the image, which likely has no shared layers, unless your base image is also using chunkah".
facts.impact: This is the whole answer to 'make removal real'. Without a flatten/rechunk step, `dnf remove` in a derived layer only writes whiteouts — the bytes still ship in the parent layer. With it, removed files are genuinely absent. Cost: first push after switching uploads the entire image.

facts.claim: `prev-ref` keeps deltas small by reusing the PREVIOUS BUILD'S LAYER PLAN, which rechunk embeds in the previous image's manifest. 3_chunk.sh does `skopeo inspect docker://${PREV_REF} > $PREV_MANIFEST` and passes `--previous-manifest`. On a first run rechunk computes a full package->layer assignment (a ~30s N^2 changelog-heuristic bin-packing); on later runs it starts from the previous plan and only runs the last placement step, which minimizes layer shifts.
facts.evidence: readme.md §4 verbatim: "The process above is only performed in the first run. In following runs, rechunk begins with the previous image plan (which is bundled into the previous image manifest) and only performs the last step. Re-using the previous plan minimizes layer shifts, which lowers layer invalidation and the subsequent download size." 3_chunk.sh (read in full) implements the skopeo fetch + `--previous-manifest` arg, with a 5-attempt retry loop.
facts.impact: Point prev-ref at your own published stable tag (e.g. ghcr.io/you/img:stable), not at the upstream base. A missing prev-ref is non-fatal by default (build continues, plan is recomputed, all layers shift, users redownload everything) — set `prev-ref-fail: 1` if you want that to be a hard error.

facts.claim: rechunk is effectively unmaintained: latest release v1.2.4 on 2025-10-11, last commit 5fbe1d3a 2025-10-11 ("bump bootc"), repo pushed_at 2025-10-11. 45 stars, 7 open issues. Its action.yml itself warns the pinned rechunk container image expires: "FIXME: old versions will expire after 90 days, so you might have to fork this action to your org's page or update every few months."
facts.evidence: gh api repos/hhd-dev/rechunk (pushed_at 2025-10-11T15:44:57Z), /releases and /commits listings, and the `rechunk` input description in action.yml.
facts.impact: If you adopt it, pin BOTH the action SHA and the container image tag, and vendor/mirror ghcr.io/hhd-dev/rechunk:v1.2.4 into your own registry. The 90-day expiry FIXME is a real build-breaker.

facts.claim: ublue-os has largely MOVED OFF the hhd-dev/rechunk action as of 2026-09. ublue-os/bazzite and ublue-os/image-template use `rpm-ostree compose build-chunked-oci --bootc`; ublue-os/aurora has a step literally named "Rechunk Image with Chunkah" (coreos/chunkah); ublue-os/bazzite-gdx has the hhd-dev/rechunk step COMMENTED OUT in its template. Only ublue-os/bluefin still runs rechunk's scripts, and via a vendored fork image `ghcr.io/ublue-os/legacy-rechunk:v1.0.1-x86_64@sha256:2627cbf...`, not the upstream action.
facts.evidence: ublue-os/bazzite .github/workflows/build.yml step "Run Rechunker" invokes `podman run ... --entrypoint /usr/bin/rpm-ostree localhost/raw-img compose build-chunked-oci --bootc --max-layers 127 --format-version 2 ...`. ublue-os/aurora .github/workflows/reusable-build.yml step name "Rechunk Image with Chunkah". ublue-os/image-template .github/workflows/build.yml: "- name: Rechunk with rpm-ostree / run: just ostree-rechunk" with a commented alternative "# If you are feeling adventurous, use the new distro agnostic rechunker / # https://github.com/coreos/chunkah". ublue-os/bluefin Justfile line 2 pins rechunker_image to ghcr.io/ublue-os/legacy-rechunk. ublue-os/bazzite-gdx build.yml lines 105-114 are all comment-prefixed.
facts.impact: If the goal is 'do what ublue does', the answer today is `rpm-ostree compose build-chunked-oci` (already in the base image) or chunkah — not the rechunk action. Both are simpler: no OSTree round-trip, no Ubuntu-24.04 pin, and chunkah needs no privileged podman.

facts.claim: `chunkah` is now SHIPPED INSIDE the fedora-bootc standard base image, with the stated purpose of rechunking.
facts.evidence:
gitlab.com/fedora/bootc/base-images standard.yaml verbatim: "packages:
  # Make Ansible "package" builtin work by default
  - python3-libdnf5
  # Content-based container layer splitting for rechunking
  # Note we should be able to move this back to the base standard/manifest.yaml
  # once chunkah is in CentOS Stream and RHEL.
  - chunkah"
facts.impact: On a fedora-bootc-derived image you can run the rechunker from inside the image itself in a multi-stage build — no external action, no rootful podman on the runner.

facts.claim: The correct removal command inside a Fedora bootc Containerfile today is `dnf remove` / `dnf5 remove` (dnf5 is what `dnf` is on Fedora). rpm-ostree is still present but is the CLIENT-SIDE tool; upstream only recommends `rpm-ostree override replace` / `override remove` for KERNEL management on OLDER images that lack kernel-install integration.
facts.evidence: Fedora bootc docs building-containers.adoc verbatim: "If you are on an older image, you can use `rpm-ostree override replace` or `rpm-ostree override remove pkg --install new-pkg` to manage your kernel." dnf.adoc verbatim: "Many examples use `RUN dnf install`. There is nothing special about the use of `dnf` in a bootc-derived container versus an application container; it is exactly the same code." Fedora Change DNFAndBootcInImageModeFedora: "rpm-ostree will still be present... the main tool for package layering on the client side."
facts.impact: Use `dnf5 remove -y` in the Containerfile. Do not reach for `rpm-ostree override remove` at build time.

facts.claim: `rpm-ostree override remove <pkg>` does NOT delete bytes — the content stays in /ostree/repo, it is merely hidden from the generated derived commit. It is also client-side state, undone by `rpm-ostree override reset`.
facts.evidence: coreos/rpm-ostree docs/administrator-handbook.md verbatim: "You can also just simply remove a base package with `rpm-ostree override remove <pkg>`. It will still be present in the underlying OSTree repository in `/ostree/repo`, but it will not be visible in the generated derived commit. Similar to the `override replace` case, using `rpm-ostree override reset` will undo the change."
facts.impact: Rules out override remove as a size-reduction mechanism entirely, at build time or runtime.

facts.claim: Deleting a file in a derived layer never reduces pull size on its own: the removal is recorded as a whiteout entry, and the original bytes remain in the parent layer. This is the core reason a flatten/rechunk pass is mandatory for removals to be 'real'.
facts.evidence: hhd-dev/rechunk readme.md states the fix side of this directly ("flattens the file system tree, thereby removing files that were replaced in later OCI layers"). coreos/chunkah README Motivation section describes the same postprocessing rationale. This is also standard OCI layer semantics (overlayfs whiteouts).
facts.impact: Any 'we removed 900MB' claim measured with `podman image inspect .Size` on a pre-rechunk image is fiction. Measure after the rechunk step, on the pushed manifest.

facts.claim: To remove a package whose dependency closure would drag out half the system, the documented Fedora-bootc-sanctioned tools are, in increasing order of violence: (1) `dnf5 remove --no-autoremove` ("Disable removal of dependencies that are no longer used"); (2) a single `dnf shell` transaction that removes and installs atomically — upstream's own kernel-rt example does exactly this; (3) `dnf swap` to a dummy/generic provider (ublue-os/aurora does `dnf -y swap fedora-logos generic-logos`); (4) `rpm --erase <pkg> --nodeps` (ublue-os/main does this for the kernel).
facts.evidence: dnf5 remove(8): "--no-autoremove: Disable removal of dependencies that are no longer used." Fedora bootc building-containers.adoc verbatim: "(echo 'remove kernel kernel-modules-core'; echo 'install kernel-rt-modules-extra kernel-rt-modules-kvm'; echo run) | dnf -y shell". ublue-os/aurora build_scripts/base/01-packages.sh: "dnf -y swap fedora-logos generic-logos" with comment "Keep *-logos in RPM DB for downstream package installations / We are not allowed to ship an empty fedora-logos package". ublue-os/main build_files/install.sh: "for pkg in kernel kernel-core kernel-modules kernel-modules-core kernel-modules-extra; do rpm --erase $pkg --nodeps; done".
facts.impact: `rpm -e --nodeps` is used in production by ublue but ONLY where something else immediately satisfies the dependency (they reinstall signed kernel RPMs on the next line). Using it to orphan a dep leaves an rpmdb that any later `dnf install` will try to repair.

facts.claim: dnf refuses to remove 'protected' packages, and the protection is transitive in the sense that a removal transaction that would pull in a protected package fails entirely. Default is `protected_packages = dnf5,glob:/etc/dnf/protected.d/*.conf` plus the running kernel via `protect_running_kernel` (default True). Removing a desktop group historically fails with exactly this.
facts.evidence: dnf5 doc/dnf5.conf.5.rst verbatim: "``protected_packages`` ... This append list option contains names of packages that DNF5 should never completely remove. They are protected via Obsoletes as well as user/plugin removals. ... Default: ``dnf5,glob:/etc/dnf/protected.d/*.conf``." and "``protect_running_kernel`` ... Default: ``True``." RH Bugzilla 1359482 "Trying to remove 'KDE Plasma Workspaces' group using dnf tries to remove systemd and dnf" — error text "Error: The operation would result in removing the following protected packages: systemd, dnf."
facts.impact: Plan for `rm -f /etc/dnf/protected.d/*.conf` or `--setopt=protected_packages=` in the build stage before a large DE removal, and re-add afterwards if you care. Note protect_running_kernel is irrelevant in a container build (no running kernel of that version), but protected.d is very relevant.

facts.claim: `clean_requirements_on_remove` defaults to True and `install_weak_deps` defaults to True. A removed package can be silently re-added by a LATER `dnf install` in the same Containerfile if any installed package Recommends it.
facts.evidence: dnf5 doc/dnf5.conf.5.rst verbatim: "``clean_requirements_on_remove`` ... If enabled, DNF5 will remove dependencies that are no longer used during ``dnf remove``. ... Default: ``True``." and "``install_weak_deps`` ... If enabled, when a new package is about to be installed, all packages linked by weak dependency relation (Recommends or Supplements flags) with this package will be pulled into the transaction. Default: ``True``."
facts.impact: Order matters: do all removals LAST, or set `--setopt=install_weak_deps=False` on every install, or add the removed names to `excludepkgs`. This is the #1 way a 'removed' package quietly comes back inside your own build.

facts.claim: Fedora bootc docs explicitly forbid `dnf -y update`/`upgrade` in a derived build, and give a second reason that bears directly on removals coming back: repo content floats, so today's build and tomorrow's build differ.
facts.evidence: building-containers.adoc verbatim: "Do *not* attempt to invoke `dnf -y update` (or `upgrade`) in general. While some things will work correctly, others will not (especially at the moment kernel and bootloader updates). ... The secondary reason to avoid this: Often people choose image-based updates for their predicability, and you can easily \"pin\" the base image by digest for example. The default for dnf repositories is to \"float\" - so what happens with an image build today could be different tomorrow. Packages can be locked with extra effort."
facts.impact: Pin the base image by digest and use dnf5 versionlock (ublue-os/main does `dnf5 versionlock add "${OVERRIDES[@]}"`) if you need a removal to stay removed across upstream base rebuilds.

facts.claim: The canonical upstream bootc KIOSK example builds UP from a minimal base rather than stripping a desktop down. gitlab.com/fedora/bootc/examples/kiosk installs gdm + firefox + gnome-kiosk-script-session onto centos-bootc and sets `systemctl set-default graphical.target`.
facts.evidence: gitlab.com/fedora/bootc/examples kiosk/Containerfile verbatim: "FROM quay.io/centos-bootc/centos-bootc-dev:stream9 / RUN rpm-ostree install gdm firefox gnome-kiosk-script-session plymouth-system-theme firewalld / ... / RUN systemctl enable sshd && firewall-offline-cmd --disabled / RUN systemctl set-default graphical.target". Note this example is old (uses rpm-ostree install and stream9).
facts.impact: Strongly suggests reframing 'remove plasma from a KDE base' as 'start from fedora-bootc minimal/standard and add cage + your app'. The removal path is the expensive, fragile one.

facts.claim: The fedora-bootc MINIMAL base image is described by its own manifest as "Effectively just bootc, systemd, kernel, and dnf as a starting point", plus coreutils, /usr/bin/dnf, selinux-policy-targeted, container-selinux, tpm2-tools, with `recommends: false`. It does NOT include NetworkManager in that explicit list.
facts.evidence: gitlab.com/fedora/bootc/base-images minimal/manifest.yaml verbatim, read in full: metadata.summary is exactly that string; `recommends: false`; packages list is coreutils, /usr/bin/dnf, selinux-policy-targeted, container-selinux, tpm2-tools; includes kernel.yaml, bootc.yaml, bootupd.yaml, ostree.yaml, initramfs.yaml, systemd-presets.yaml etc.
facts.impact: This is the real floor for 'what must survive'. Anything you strip below this and the image stops being a bootc image. Use it as the target size to compare your stripped-KDE image against — if stripping doesn't get you near it, rebuild from it instead.

facts.claim: cage, greetd, seatd, weston and gnome-kiosk all exist as Fedora 43 packages: cage 0.2.0 ("A Wayland kiosk"), greetd 0.10.3 ("A generic greeter daemon"), seatd 0.9.3 ("Minimal seat management daemon"), weston 14.0.2, gnome-kiosk 49.0. cagebreak is NOT packaged.
facts.evidence: mdapi.fedoraproject.org/f43/pkg/{cage,greetd,seatd,weston,gnome-kiosk,cagebreak} — first five return versions/summaries as quoted; cagebreak returns not found.
facts.impact: cage is the right compositor for single-app kiosk. greetd is optional — for a true kiosk you can skip the greeter entirely and run cage from a systemd service, which removes greetd + its PAM session from the surviving set.

facts.claim: rechunk's 1_prune.sh merges /etc/passwd and /etc/group into /usr/lib/passwd and /usr/lib/group (nss-altfiles). ublue-os had to ship a boot-time repair unit because users who rebase AWAY from a rechunked image get black screens and unbootable systems.
facts.evidence: ublue-os/aurora system_files/shared/usr/lib/systemd/system/rechunker-group-fix.service verbatim header: "We have this script so that people using images with `nss-altfiles` (`/usr/lib/g{roup,shadow}`) do not break their systems when rebasing to an image without that. This usually happens when using https://github.com/hhd-dev/rechunk then rebasing to an image without it. Please DO NOT remove this unless this is fully, completely obsolete. This is exactly what is making it break: https://github.com/ublue-os/legacy-rechunk/blob/1d2b0c2e.../1_prune.sh#L41-L47 Users WILL experience black screens and systems will NOT boot if this script malfunctions." It links bootc-dev/bootc#1179, ublue-os/main#759, bluefin-lts#918, image-template#177, aurora#1468, bluefin#3852. Created 2025-12-16.
facts.impact: A real, severe, production-observed gotcha specific to rechunk (not chunkah, not build-chunked-oci). If you adopt rechunk you inherit this migration hazard for anyone rebasing off your image.

facts.claim: `skopeo inspect` (non-raw) returns a `LayersData` array with a per-layer `Size` field, which is the COMPRESSED registry blob size. Summing it gives the cold-pull byte count.
facts.evidence: containers/skopeo docs/skopeo-inspect.1.md, EXAMPLES section, verbatim output includes: "\"LayersData\": [ { \"MIMEType\": \"application/vnd.docker.image.rootfs.diff.tar.gzip\", \"Digest\": \"sha256:cb8b...\", \"Size\": 65990920, \"Annotations\": null } ]". `--raw` is documented as "Output raw manifest or config data depending on --config option."
facts.impact: This is the number to report as 'pull size'. `podman image inspect --format '{{.Size}}'` is the UNCOMPRESSED on-disk size and will be 2-3x larger — don't mix them up in a savings claim.

facts.claim: rpm's installed-size query tags are `SIZE` (int32, "Installed package size") and `LONGSIZE` (int64, "Installed package size when > 4GB"). rpm's own docs say to always use the Long* variants.
facts.evidence: rpm-software-management/rpm docs/manual/tags.md verbatim table rows: "Size | 1009 | int32 | Installed package size." and "Longsize | 5009 | int64 | Installed package size when > 4GB." plus "These tags provide 64bit values regardless of underlying storage size. ... Always use these to access the sizes."
facts.impact: Use %{LONGSIZE} not %{SIZE} in the query format. Note this is the UNCOMPRESSED installed footprint — it is an upper bound on, not equal to, compressed pull-size savings.

facts.claim: dnf5 repoquery supports `--queryformat` with an `installsize` tag and an `--installed` filter, which is an alternative to rpm -qa for per-package size.
facts.evidence: dnf5 repoquery(8) docs: "--queryformat ... Display format for packages. The <format> string can contain tags (%{<tag>}) which are replaced with corresponding attributes of the package. Default is \"%{full_nevra}\"." and tag "installsize - Display install size of the package." and "--installed: Query installed packages."
facts.impact: Useful when you want to size a package that is NOT yet installed (planning a removal target) — repoquery without --installed gives installsize from the repo metadata.

facts.claim: `rpm-ostree compose build-chunked-oci` requires `--bootc`, takes exactly one of `--from` / `--rootfs`, defaults to `--format-version=1`, and automatically reuses existing layers when the `--output` image was previously chunked. Format 2 is recommended for reproducible builds.
facts.evidence: coreos/rpm-ostree docs/build-chunked-oci.md verbatim: "Currently the `--bootc` option is required." / "the `--from` and `--rootfs` options are mutually-exclusive; exactly one is required" / "When composing an image from an image that was previously chunked, the existing image's layers will automatically be re-used when specifying it as the `--output` image." / "The default value is `--format-version=1` for backwards-compatibility" / "If reproducible builds are desirable, it is recommended to use `--format-version=2`."
facts.impact: The `--output` reuse behaviour is build-chunked-oci's equivalent of rechunk's prev-ref, and it is automatic. ublue-os/bazzite uses `--max-layers 127 --format-version 2`; image-template uses `--max-layers 127 --format-version=2`.

facts.claim: chunkah can rechunk an OSTree-based bootc image by turning it into a plain one with `--prune /sysroot/` and stripping the stale ostree labels with `--label ostree.commit- --label ostree.final-diffid-`. Default max layers is 64; 128 is recommended for bootable images. It runs as a normal (non-privileged) container in a multi-stage build.
facts.evidence: coreos/chunkah README, "Compatibility with bootable (bootc) images" section verbatim: "Using chunkah to rechunk an OSTree-based bootc image is also possible by transforming it into a plain one by passing `--prune /sysroot/` to strip OSTree data from the image. If base metadata is persisted ... you will need to remove the ostree-related labels using the `--label KEY-` option" plus the full Dockerfile example, and "You will likely want to increase the default maximum number of layers from 64 (e.g. 128)". Also: "labels from the base image will be lost, including versioning information and `containers.bootc=1`, which is required by bootc."
facts.impact: chunkah is the low-friction option: no sudo, no Ubuntu-24.04 pin, works in `buildah build`. But you MUST re-add `containers.bootc=1` (via CHUNKAH_CONFIG_STR or --label) or the output is not a bootc image.

facts.claim: The Containerfile-level lever for removing individual FILES from a package you must keep is only available in the base-image treefile layer (`remove-from-packages`), not in a derived Containerfile. In a derived Containerfile you delete the files with `rm` and rely on the rechunk pass to make it real.
facts.evidence: gitlab.com/fedora/bootc/base-images minimal/manifest.yaml verbatim: "remove-from-packages:\n  # Generally we expect other tools to do this (e.g. Ignition or cloud-init)\n  - [systemd, /usr/lib/systemd/system/sysinit.target.wants/systemd-firstboot.service]". No equivalent exists in dnf5 or in the bootc Containerfile docs.
facts.impact: For 'keep the package, drop its 400MB of data files', plain `rm -rf` + rechunk is the derived-image answer. rpm -V will then report the package as modified; nothing enforces it.

# NOT copied verbatim from upstream; assembled from dnf5 docs + ublue practice.
# Each primitive is individually verified; the combination is mine.
FROM ghcr.io/ublue-os/kinoite-main@sha256:<pin-me> AS build

RUN <<'EOF'
set -xeuo pipefail

# 1. dnf refuses to touch anything listed in protected.d. Stash, don't delete,
#    so you can restore before the final stage if you care.
mkdir -p /tmp/protected.bak && mv /etc/dnf/protected.d/*.conf /tmp/protected.bak/ || true

# 2. See what the blast radius IS before committing. --assumeno prints the full
#    transaction table incl. the "Freed space" line and exits non-zero.
dnf5 remove --assumeno plasma-workspace || true

# 3. Remove. --no-autoremove keeps the shared deps that the survivors need;
#    drop it (default) if you want dnf to garbage-collect orphans for you.
dnf5 remove -y --no-autoremove \
      plasma-workspace plasma-desktop plasma-workspace-wayland \
      kwin kwin-wayland sddm sddm-kcm \
      plasma-systemsettings plasma-discover discover-flatpak \
      kde-settings kde-settings-plasma

# 4. Stop them ever coming back: a later `dnf install` pulls Recommends by
#    default (install_weak_deps=True), and that is the #1 way a removed
#    package silently returns.
cat >/etc/dnf/libdnf5.conf.d/99-no-plasma.conf <<'CONF'
[main]
install_weak_deps=False
excludepkgs=plasma-*,kwin*,sddm*,kde-settings*
CONF

# 5. Install the survivors AFTER the removal, with weak deps off.
dnf5 install -y --setopt=install_weak_deps=False \
      cage seatd NetworkManager

mv /tmp/protected.bak/*.conf /etc/dnf/protected.d/ || true
dnf clean all
EOF

# 6. Verify inside the build, so a regression fails the build rather than ships.
RUN <<'EOF'
set -xeuo pipefail
! rpm -q plasma-workspace kwin sddm 2>/dev/null | grep -qv 'is not installed'
test ! -e /usr/bin/kwin_wayland
test ! -d /usr/share/plasma
bootc container lint
EOF

# 7. THE STEP THAT MAKES THE REMOVAL REAL. Without this the deleted bytes are
#    still in the parent layer behind a whiteout and nobody's pull gets smaller.
FROM quay.io/coreos/chunkah AS chunkah
ARG CHUNKAH_CONFIG_STR
RUN --mount=from=build,src=/,target=/chunkah,ro \
    --mount=type=bind,target=/run/src,rw \
      chunkah build --prune /sysroot/ --max-layers 128 \
        --label ostree.commit- --label ostree.final-diffid- \
        --output oci:/run/src/out

FROM oci:out

snippets.code:
IMG=docker://ghcr.io/myorg/myimage:latest

# COMPRESSED pull size (sum of registry blob sizes). This is the number to report.
skopeo inspect "$IMG" | jq '[.LayersData[].Size] | add' | numfmt --to=iec

# Same from the raw manifest
skopeo inspect --raw "$IMG" | jq '[.layers[].size] | add' | numfmt --to=iec

# Per-layer breakdown, largest first
skopeo inspect "$IMG" \
  | jq -r '.LayersData[] | "\(.Size)\t\(.Digest)"' \
  | sort -rn | numfmt --to=iec --field=1 | head -20

# If it is a multi-arch INDEX, .layers is absent -- resolve the arch first
skopeo inspect --raw "$IMG" | jq -r '.manifests[]? | "\(.platform.architecture)\t\(.digest)"'
skopeo inspect --raw docker://ghcr.io/myorg/myimage@sha256:<arch-digest> \
  | jq '[.layers[].size] | add' | numfmt --to=iec

# UNCOMPRESSED on-disk size (do NOT quote this as "pull size" -- it is 2-3x larger)
podman image inspect --format '{{.Size}}' localhost/myimage:latest | numfmt --to=iec
podman image inspect --format '{{len .RootFS.Layers}}' localhost/myimage:latest

# ACTUAL DELTA an existing user downloads: bytes of layers in NEW that are not in OLD.
# This is the only honest "update size" number, and it is what prev-ref protects.
skopeo inspect docker://ghcr.io/myorg/myimage:old > /tmp/old.json
skopeo inspect docker://ghcr.io/myorg/myimage:new > /tmp/new.json
jq -n --slurpfile o /tmp/old.json --slurpfile n /tmp/new.json '
  ($o[0].LayersData | map(.Digest)) as $old
  | [ $n[0].LayersData[] | select(.Digest as $d | ($old | index($d)) | not) | .Size ]
  | { new_layers: length, delta_bytes: (add // 0) }' \
  | jq '.delta_human = (.delta_bytes/1048576 | floor | tostring + " MiB")'

# Before/after savings in one line
before=$(skopeo inspect docker://ghcr.io/myorg/myimage:before | jq '[.LayersData[].Size]|add')
after=$(skopeo  inspect docker://ghcr.io/myorg/myimage:after  | jq '[.LayersData[].Size]|add')
echo "saved $(( (before-after)/1048576 )) MiB ($(( (before-after)*100/before ))%)"

gotchas: rechunk has no `rawhide` input. Passing one does nothing (or errors). Verified by reading action.yml and grepping the whole repo — zero hits for rawhide/RAWHIDE.

rechunk's output is named `location`, not `output`. The ublue-os/bazzite-gdx template that people copy has `steps.rechunk.outputs.output` in its commented block — that expands to empty and the `sudo rm -rf` there becomes `rm -rf ` (harmless, but the cleanup silently never happens and you run out of runner disk).
rechunk needs `runs-on: ubuntu-24.04` and ROOTFUL podman. `ubuntu-latest` and a rootless `podman build` both fail — the action does `sudo podman create <ref>` and cannot see a rootless image.

rechunk's `rechunk:` container image tag must match the action version, and upstream's own FIXME says old tags expire after 90 days. Mirror ghcr.io/hhd-dev/rechunk:v1.2.4 into your registry or builds will break on a schedule you do not control.

Severe, production-observed: rechunk's 1_prune.sh merges /etc/passwd and /etc/group into /usr/lib/passwd and /usr/lib/group (nss-altfiles). Users who later rebase OFF a rechunked image get black screens and unbootable systems. ublue-os ships a boot-time repair unit (aurora rechunker-group-fix.service, created 2025-12-16) whose header says "Users WILL experience black screens and systems will NOT boot if this script malfunctions", linking six separate issues. chunkah and rpm-ostree build-chunked-oci do not have this problem.

A missing prev-ref is NOT fatal by default — rechunk logs "Continuing build without previous manifest", recomputes the plan from scratch, and every layer shifts, so every user redownloads the whole image. If you care, set `prev-ref-fail: 1`. Point prev-ref at YOUR published tag, never at the upstream base.

install_weak_deps defaults to True. Any `dnf install` placed AFTER your `dnf remove` can pull the removed package straight back as a Recommends. Do removals last, or set install_weak_deps=False, or add the names to excludepkgs. This is the most common way a 'removed' package is still in the shipped image.

protected_packages defaults to `dnf5,glob:/etc/dnf/protected.d/*.conf`. Removing a desktop group hits this immediately — the canonical failure is RH bz#1359482, "Error: The operation would result in removing the following protected packages: systemd, dnf." You have to move /etc/dnf/protected.d/*.conf aside in the build stage.

`rpm-ostree override remove` is not a build-time command and saves zero bytes even at runtime: upstream docs say the package "will still be present in the underlying OSTree repository in /ostree/repo, but it will not be visible in the generated derived commit", and `override reset` undoes it.

`rpm -e --nodeps` leaves an rpmdb with unsatisfied Requires. ublue-os only uses it where a replacement is installed on the very next line. Any later dnf transaction in the same build may try to 'fix' the hole by reinstalling what you removed.

Deleting files in a derived layer does not shrink the pull. Whiteouts mask; parent layers still carry the bytes. If you report savings from `podman image inspect .Size` on the pre-rechunk image, the number is wrong. Measure `skopeo inspect | jq '[.LayersData[].Size]|add'` on the PUSHED manifest.

chunkah in the build-time `FROM oci:` flow LOSES base-image labels including `containers.bootc=1`, which bootc requires. Pass CHUNKAH_CONFIG_STR or re-add the label, or you ship a non-bootable image that builds and pushes fine.
chunkah's buildah flow needs `--skip-unused-stages=false` and cannot use `--jobs`. Buildah <1.44 additionally needs `-v $(pwd):/run/src --security-opt=label=disable`.

`rpm-ostree compose build-chunked-oci` defaults to `--format-version=1`, which produces sparse layers with non-reproducible implicit parent directories. ublue uses `--format-version 2`. Switching format versions breaks layer reuse against previously-published images.

Fedora bootc docs: "Do *not* attempt to invoke `dnf -y update` (or `upgrade`) in general" — and note the second reason they give, that repos float, which is also why a removal that worked today can behave differently tomorrow against the same base tag. Pin the base by digest.

Use %{LONGSIZE} not %{SIZE} in rpm query formats; rpm's own docs say "Always use these to access the sizes." And remember installed size is uncompressed — it is an upper bound on compressed pull savings, typically by 2-3x.
`skopeo inspect --raw` on a multi-arch tag returns an index with `.manifests[]` and no `.layers`, so `jq '[.layers[].size]|add'` silently yields null. Resolve the per-arch digest first.
bootc images have ENTRYPOINT /sbin/init. `podman run --rm IMG rpm -qa` will not do what you want — use `--entrypoint rpm`.
blockers: The question's premise that rechunk takes a `rawhide` input is FALSE. I read action.yml in full and grepped the entire repo (including 3_chunk.sh and all of src/rechunk/): there is no rawhide input, no RAWHIDE env var, no mention anywhere. The real inputs are ref, prev-ref, clear-plan, prev-ref-fail, max-layers, skip_compression, labels, description, version, pretty, rechunk, keep-ref, changelog, git, revision, formatters, meta. Any plan written against a `rawhide:` input needs rewriting.

The premise that hhd-dev/rechunk is what ublue-os uses is now largely FALSE, as of 2026-09. ublue-os/bazzite and ublue-os/image-template run `rpm-ostree compose build-chunked-oci --bootc`; ublue-os/aurora's step is literally named "Rechunk Image with Chunkah" (coreos/chunkah); ublue-os/bazzite-gdx ships the rechunk step COMMENTED OUT. Only ublue-os/bluefin still runs rechunk's scripts, and via a vendored fork (ghcr.io/ublue-os/legacy-rechunk) rather than the upstream action. Recommend building the plan on `rpm-ostree compose build-chunked-oci` (already present in fedora-bootc) or chunkah (now SHIPPED IN the fedora-bootc standard base image per its standard.yaml), not on the rechunk action.

hhd-dev/rechunk appears unmaintained: last release v1.2.4 and last commit both 2025-10-11, ~11 months before today. Its own action.yml carries a FIXME warning that the container images it depends on expire after 90 days. Adopting it means taking on maintenance of a fork.

The framing "remove a WHOLE desktop environment from a KDE base image" runs against how upstream solves this. The canonical Fedora bootc kiosk example (gitlab.com/fedora/bootc/examples/kiosk) builds UP from centos-bootc and installs a kiosk session; it does not strip a DE. The fedora-bootc MINIMAL base exists precisely for this and describes itself as "Effectively just bootc, systemd, kernel, and dnf as a starting point." Stripping Plasma out of Kinoite means fighting protected_packages, weak deps, and a dependency closure that historically tries to remove systemd and dnf (RH bz#1359482), for a result that will still be larger than fedora-bootc minimal + cage. Recommend inverting: start from fedora-bootc minimal or standard, add kernel/firmware, NetworkManager, seatd, cage, and your app. If the KDE base is non-negotiable for some other reason, say so, because it roughly doubles the work.

I could not find a primary source documenting a specific incident of "an upstream rebuild re-added a removed package" in a bootc image. What I CAN document as the mechanism is three verified things: install_weak_deps=True pulling a removal back inside your own build; dnf repos floating so the same base tag resolves differently day to day (stated explicitly in the Fedora bootc docs as a reason to avoid dnf update); and protected_packages/comps-group membership. Treat the specific 'upstream rebuild re-adds it' story as unverified — the defensible mitigations are pinning the base by digest, dnf5 versionlock, excludepkgs, and a build-time assertion step that fails the build if the package reappears.

The minimal surviving package set for a Plasma-stripped kiosk is my synthesis, not something I found written down. I verified the base floor (fedora-bootc minimal manifest) and that cage 0.2.0, greetd 0.10.3, seatd 0.9.3, weston 14.0.2 and gnome-kiosk 49.0 exist in Fedora 43. I did NOT verify by booting that Plasma-minus-everything plus cage actually boots. Budget a VM boot test (ublue does this with dgoss and corral in CI) before committing to a size target.

area: GitHub Actions constraints for building + VM-testing bootc images on free public-repo runners (as of 2026-09-20)

facts.claim: /dev/kvm EXISTS on standard free GitHub-hosted Linux runners (not just larger runners). GitHub shipped hardware-accelerated virtualization to the standard 2-vCPU Linux runners; users independently confirmed /dev/kvm present on all free/non-large ubuntu-latest runners after the 2024-01-17 runner update. It is still gated by device permissions, not by absence.
facts.evidence: https://github.blog/changelog/2024-04-02-github-actions-hardware-accelerated-android-virtualization-now-available/ — 'Actions users of our 2-vCPU GitHub-hosted Linux runners will be able to make use of hardware acceleration'. Corroborated by https://github.com/orgs/community/discussions/160591 (alexvanyo, 2024-01-18): 'Since the runner update yesterday, I am seeing that /dev/kvm exists for _all_ free/non-large ubuntu-latest runners.'
facts.impact: VM-booting the built qcow2 on a free runner is feasible. Budget for `qemu-system-x86_64 -enable-kvm` to actually accelerate; do not design around TCG-only emulation.

facts.claim: The required enablement step is a udev rule making /dev/kvm mode 0666 — NOT `sudo usermod -aG kvm $USER`. usermod is the wrong tool because a supplementary group added mid-job does not apply to the already-running shell (no re-login), so the device stays unreadable.
facts.evidence: Verbatim from GitHub's own changelog and from ReactiveCircus/android-emulator-runner README (the canonical consumer): `echo 'KERNEL=="kvm", GROUP="kvm", MODE="0666", OPTIONS+="static_node=kvm"' | sudo tee /etc/udev/rules.d/99-kvm4all.rules; sudo udevadm control --reload-rules; sudo udevadm trigger --name-match=kvm`
facts.impact: Use the exact 3-line udev snippet as a step before any QEMU step. Skip usermod entirely.

facts.claim: qemu-kvm / qemu-system-x86 is NOT preinstalled on the ubuntu-24.04 or ubuntu-26.04 runner images — you must apt-install it.
facts.evidence: Grepped https://raw.githubusercontent.com/actions/runner-images/main/images/ubuntu/Ubuntu2404-Readme.md and Ubuntu2604-Readme.md for 'kvm|qemu|libvirt|virtual' — zero matches in either manifest.
facts.impact: Add `sudo apt-get install -y qemu-system-x86 qemu-utils cloud-image-utils ovmf` (~60-90s) before the VM test step.

facts.claim: DISK IS NOT A HARD BLOCKER. The upstream osbuild bootc-image-builder-action's own CI builds raw+qcow2+vmdk+vhd (and separately anaconda-iso) from quay.io/fedora/fedora-silverblue:latest on a FREE `ubuntu-24.04` runner, with a 45-minute timeout, using one disk-cleanup step.
facts.evidence: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/osbuild/bootc-image-builder-action/main/.github/workflows/ci.yml — job `test-action`: `runs-on: ubuntu-24.04`, `timeout-minutes: 45`, step `Maximize Build Space` uses `ublue-os/remove-unwanted-software@cc0becac701cf642c8f0a6613bbdaf5dc36b259e # v9` with `remove-codeql: true`, matrix types `raw qcow2 vmdk vhd` and `anaconda-iso`.
facts.impact: Directly refutes the 'potential hard blocker' premise. Copy this exact pattern (ubuntu-24.04 + remove-unwanted-software v9) rather than inventing a cleanup script.

facts.claim: GitHub's own runner docs table ('14 GB SSD' for ubuntu-latest) is misleading and understates usable space. The real root filesystem is ~84 GB with roughly 25-29 GB free before cleanup; the 14 GB figure corresponds to the separate temp disk.
facts.evidence: docs.github.com/en/actions/reference/runners/github-hosted-runners public-repo table: ubuntu-latest/24.04/26.04 = 4 CPU, 16 GB RAM, 14 GB SSD. Contradicted by https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ublue-os/remove-unwanted-software/master/README.md: 'public shared Github runners come with around 25-29 GB of free disk space' and 'a 84GB OS disk on / and a 14GB temp disk mounted on /mnt'.
facts.impact: Do not size the build against 14 GB. Still emit `df -h` before and after cleanup in CI so a future runner-image change surfaces immediately instead of as a mid-build ENOSPC.

facts.claim: ublue-os/remove-unwanted-software frees ~36 GB with its defaults, itemized per-toggle, taking total available to roughly 51 GB.
facts.evidence: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ublue-os/remove-unwanted-software/v9/action.yml input descriptions: remove-dotnet '~2 GB', remove-android '~9 GB', remove-haskell '~5.2 GB', remove-codeql '~5.4 GB', remove-docker-images '~3.2 GB', remove-large-packages '~3.1 GB', remove-cached-tools '~8.3 GB', remove-swapfile '~4 GB' (default false). README: 'you'll get around 51 GB of disk space available'.
facts.impact: Sum = ~36.2 GB without the swapfile. Leave remove-swapfile at false — a bootc build under memory pressure will be OOM-killed with no error naming the action.

facts.claim: A Fedora KDE bootc image is ~3.7 GB COMPRESSED in the registry. Measured directly against GHCR: ghcr.io/ublue-os/aurora:latest (Fedora KDE bootc) = 256 layers, 3.71 GB compressed; ghcr.io/ublue-os/bluefin:latest (GNOME) = 75 layers, 3.32 GB.
facts.evidence: Anonymous GHCR token + manifest pull, summed layer sizes: `curl https://ghcr.io/token?scope=repository:ublue-os/aurora:pull` then GET /v2/ublue-os/aurora/manifests/latest → 256 layers totalling 3.71e9 bytes.
facts.impact: Uncompressed in containers storage this lands around 9-11 GB; plus a sparse qcow2 of similar order, the peak is ~25-30 GB. That fits inside ~51 GB post-cleanup but NOT inside the ~25-29 GB baseline. Cleanup is mandatory, not optional.

facts.claim: bootc-image-builder does NOT need /dev/kvm to produce a qcow2. It needs a privileged podman container with host container storage bind-mounted. KVM only enters for the experimental rootless `--in-vm` path.
facts.evidence: https://github.com/osbuild/bootc-image-builder README: `sudo podman run --rm -it --privileged --pull=newer --security-opt label=type:unconfined_t -v ./config.toml:/config.toml:ro -v ./output:/output -v /var/lib/containers/storage:/var/lib/containers/storage quay.io/centos-bootc/bootc-image-builder:latest --type qcow2 --use-librepo=True <image>`. KVM is mentioned only as: 'To perform a rootless build KVM is used.'
facts.impact: Split the concern: the BUILD job needs no KVM (so it can run anywhere); only the VM-TEST job needs the udev rule. Keeps the KVM dependency off the critical publishing path.

facts.claim: bootc-image-builder sizes the root filesystem as 'the value specified in this configuration or 2x the size of the base container, whichever is largest'.
facts.evidence: osbuild/bootc-image-builder README, filesystem customization section.
facts.impact: For a ~10 GB uncompressed KDE image the default rootfs is ~20 GB. Pin an explicit filesystem size in config.toml so the qcow2 does not silently double when the image grows.

facts.claim: CONFIRMED cosign 3.x regression: cosign 3.x defaults --new-bundle-format to TRUE, writing signatures as OCI 1.1 referrers under a `sha256-<digest>` tag instead of the legacy `sha256-<digest>.sig` tag. containers/image (podman, skopeo, bootc, rpm-ostree) only discovers the legacy .sig tag and does not consult the referrers API; GHCR does not implement /referrers. Result: images sign 'successfully', `cosign verify` passes, and podman/bootc see them as unsigned.
facts.evidence: https://github.com/projectbluefin/common/issues/977 — Bluefin images built from ~2026-06-08 were effectively unsigned; cutoff correlates with a Renovate bump of sigstore/cosign-installer v3→v4 on 2026-06-04. Upstream tracker https://github.com/containers/container-libs/issues/388 (opened 2025-10-12, still OPEN): 'Cosign recently released v3 of their CLI, which switches to a new signing bundle format by default. skopeo, podman and rpm-ostree fail to verify to images with this new signature format.'
facts.impact: --new-bundle-format=false is MANDATORY. And a `cosign verify` gate in CI will not catch a regression here — add a registry-level assertion that the `sha256-<digest>.sig` tag exists.

facts.claim: In cosign v3.1.2 the flag is still accepted but is now DEPRECATED and hidden from generated docs, with default still true. Read from source: `cmd.Flags().BoolVar(&o.NewBundleFormat, "new-bundle-format", true, ...)` immediately followed by `cmd.Flags().MarkDeprecated("new-bundle-format", "this will be the only supported format in future versions")`.
facts.evidence: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/sigstore/cosign/v3.1.2/cmd/cosign/cli/options/sign.go lines 161-162. Confirmed absent from https://raw.githubusercontent.com/sigstore/cosign/v3.1.2/doc/cosign_sign.md (documented in v3.0.0's doc, gone by v3.1.2 — hidden, not removed).
facts.impact: Pin `cosign-release:` to an exact version (v3.1.2 or v3.1.3). Do NOT float, and do not let Renovate bump the major — the flag disappears in a future major and your signatures go invisible again, silently.

facts.claim: Two independent production bootc repos converge on the identical incantation: `cosign sign -y --new-bundle-format=false --use-signing-config=false --key env://COSIGN_PRIVATE_KEY <registry>/<image>@<digest>`, with cosign-installer pinned by SHA to v4.1.2 and cosign-release pinned to v3.1.2 / v3.1.3.
facts.evidence: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ublue-os/image-template/main/.github/workflows/build.yml (cosign-release 'v3.1.2') and https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Danathar/arch-bootc/main/.github/workflows/build.yml (cosign-release v3.1.3). Both carry inline comments citing containers/container-libs#388 and coreos/rpm-ostree#5509.
facts.impact: Use this verbatim. Note both use KEY-based signing, not keyless — see the keyless gotcha below.

facts.claim: cosign v3.1.x's `sign` also defaults `--use-signing-config` to true ('whether to use a TUF-provided signing config for the service URLs'), which is why the working invocations pass --use-signing-config=false alongside the bundle flag.
facts.evidence: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/sigstore/cosign/v3.1.2/doc/cosign_sign.md: '--use-signing-config  whether to use a TUF-provided signing config for the service URLs (default true)'.
facts.impact: Pass both flags together. Passing only --new-bundle-format=false is the common half-fix.

facts.claim: `--registry-referrers-mode` (allowed: legacy, oci-1-1) is a separate, long-standing flag present in cosign v2.5.3, v3.0.0 and v3.1.2 alike. It controls referrer FETCHING, not the signature bundle format, so it is not the fix for this regression.
facts.evidence: Present at doc/cosign_sign.md line ~93 in all three tags checked.
facts.impact: Some blog posts recommend --registry-referrers-mode=legacy as the fix. It is not sufficient on its own; --new-bundle-format=false is the load-bearing flag.

facts.claim: Publishing to GHCR from Actions with the built-in GITHUB_TOKEN works and needs exactly `permissions: {contents: read, packages: write, id-token: write}` (id-token only for keyless/OIDC), with docker/login-action using `username: ${{ github.actor }}` and `password: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}`.
facts.evidence: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ublue-os/image-template/main/.github/workflows/build.yml — permissions block and `docker/login-action@abd2ef45e78c5afb21d64d4ca52ee8550d9572c7 # v4.5.1` with `registry: ghcr.io`.
facts.impact: No PAT needed for pushing to GHCR in the same repo. Pin login-action by SHA as upstream does.

facts.claim: Making the GHCR package public is a manual, one-time, IRREVERSIBLE UI action — it cannot be done from the workflow. Package settings → Danger Zone → Change visibility → Public.
facts.evidence: docs.github.com/en/packages/learn-github-packages/configuring-a-packages-access-control-and-visibility: 'At the bottom of the page, under "Danger Zone", click Change visibility.' / 'To make the package visible to anyone, select Public.' / 'Once you make a package public, you cannot make it private again.'
facts.impact: Budget a manual step after the first successful push. Until then `bootc switch` from a clean machine will 401 and look like a build bug.

facts.claim: GHCR storage and bandwidth are FREE for public packages, with no quota.
facts.evidence: docs.github.com/en/packages/learn-github-packages/introduction-to-github-packages: 'GitHub Packages usage is free for public packages.' The 500 MB free-tier storage figure applies to private packages only.
facts.impact: Nightly multi-GB image pushes to a public GHCR package cost nothing. Still prune old versions to keep the package page usable.

facts.claim: GitHub Actions minutes are FREE and unmetered for public repositories on standard hosted runners. The 2,000 min/mo Free-plan allowance applies only to private repos.
facts.evidence: docs.github.com/en/billing/concepts/product-billing/github-actions: 'GitHub Actions usage is free for self-hosted runners and for public repositories that use standard GitHub-hosted runners.'
facts.impact: Minutes are not a constraint. Concurrency and the 6h wall clock are.

facts.claim: Hard limits: 6 hours max per job on hosted runners; 35 days max per workflow run (including waiting/approval); 20 concurrent jobs total on the Free plan across all standard hosted runners.
facts.evidence: docs.github.com/en/actions/reference/limits — 'If a job reaches this limit, the job is terminated and fails' (6h); 'A workflow run can continue for a maximum of 35 days'; Free plan 20 total concurrent jobs.
facts.impact: A full Fedora KDE bootc build + bib qcow2 + VM boot fits well inside 6h (upstream bib CI uses a 45-min timeout). The 20-job concurrency ceiling bites if you matrix across many flavors/architectures — cap the matrix.

facts.claim: Artifact/log retention defaults to 90 days; on PUBLIC repos the configurable range is 1-90 days (private/internal get 1-400).
facts.evidence: docs.github.com/en/actions/how-tos/manage-workflow-runs/remove-workflow-artifacts: 'By default, GitHub stores build logs and artifacts for 90 days.' Range per GitHub org-settings retention docs.
facts.impact: A multi-GB qcow2 uploaded as an artifact vanishes at 90 days max. Anything meant to persist belongs in a GitHub Release or in GHCR as an OCI artifact, not in actions/upload-artifact.

facts.claim: Scheduled workflows on PUBLIC repos ARE auto-disabled after 60 days with no repository activity, and only new commits reset the timer — a nightly build's own successful runs do not.
facts.evidence: docs.github.com/en/actions/reference/workflows-and-actions/events-that-trigger-workflows: 'In a public repository, scheduled workflows are automatically disabled when no repository activity has occurred in 60 days.' Re-enable via UI or `gh workflow enable WORKFLOW`.
facts.impact: A nightly bootc build on a stable repo WILL silently stop after 60 quiet days. Add a keepalive (commit-bump or API-based) or an external cron hitting workflow_dispatch.

facts.claim: `repository_dispatch` and `workflow_dispatch` are explicitly EXEMPT from the GITHUB_TOKEN recursion-prevention rule — they always create workflow runs even when sent with GITHUB_TOKEN. The recursion rule is therefore NOT what blocks cross-repo dispatch.
facts.evidence: docs.github.com/en/actions/how-tos/write-workflows/choose-when-workflows-run/trigger-a-workflow: 'events triggered by the GITHUB_TOKEN will not create a new workflow run, with the following exceptions: workflow_dispatch and repository_dispatch events always create workflow runs.'
facts.impact: Corrects a widespread misconception. The real blocker is token scope (next fact), which changes what you need to fix.

facts.claim: CROSS-repo dispatch still requires a PAT or GitHub App token, because GITHUB_TOKEN is scoped to the repository containing the workflow and cannot authenticate POST /repos/{other-owner}/{other-repo}/dispatches. Classic PAT needs the `repo` scope; a fine-grained PAT or App installation token needs Contents: write on the TARGET repo.
facts.evidence: docs.github.com/en/rest/repos/repos#create-a-repository-dispatch-event: 'POST /repos/{owner}/{repo}/dispatches'; 'OAuth app tokens and personal access tokens (classic) need the repo scope to use this endpoint.' Combined with GITHUB_TOKEN's documented per-repository scoping.
facts.impact: Plan for a secret. Prefer a GitHub App installation token (actions/create-github-app-token) scoped to just repo B over a classic PAT with blanket `repo` — a classic `repo` PAT grants write to every repo the user can touch.

facts.claim: A fork PR's GITHUB_TOKEN is downgraded to read-only regardless of the `permissions:` block requested in the workflow.
facts.evidence: Inline comment in https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Danathar/arch-bootc/main/.github/workflows/build.yml: 'a fork's GITHUB_TOKEN is downgraded to read-only by GitHub regardless of the `packages: write` permission requested above'.
facts.impact: Guard every GHCR-writing step with the upstream `if:` condition, or fork PRs fail with a confusing 403 rather than skipping cleanly.

facts.claim: As of 2026-09-20 `ubuntu-latest` still resolves to Ubuntu 24.04. The migration to 26.04 rolls out 2026-10-19 through 2026-11-19.
facts.evidence: https://github.blog/changelog/2026-09-17-ubuntu-26-generally-available-and-latest-migration/ and actions/runner-images issue #14748.
facts.impact: Pin `runs-on: ubuntu-24.04` (or deliberately ubuntu-26.04, as ublue-os/image-template already does) rather than ubuntu-latest — otherwise the runner image shifts under a nightly build during that window.

snippets.name: GHCR publish with the built-in GITHUB_TOKEN (verbatim from ublue-os/image-template)
snippets.code:
jobs:
  build_push:
    name: Build and push image
    runs-on: ubuntu-26.04

    permissions:
      contents: read
      packages: write
      id-token: write

    steps:
      - name: Login to GitHub Container Registry
        uses: docker/login-action@abd2ef45e78c5afb21d64d4ca52ee8550d9572c7 # v4.5.1
        if: github.event_name != 'pull_request' && github.ref == format('refs/heads/{0}', github.event.repository.default_branch)
        with:
          registry: ghcr.io
          username: ${{ github.actor }}
          password: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}

      - name: Push To GHCR
        if: github.event_name != 'pull_request' && github.ref == format('refs/heads/{0}', github.event.repository.default_branch)
        id: push-image

snippets.name: VM-test job skeleton: boot the qcow2 under KVM and assert bootc status — composed, pattern not copied verbatim from one upstream file
snippets.code:
vm-test:
  runs-on: ubuntu-24.04     # pinned: ubuntu-latest moves to 26.04 from 2026-10-19
  needs: build
  timeout-minutes: 45
  steps:
    - name: Enable KVM group perms
      run: |
        echo 'KERNEL=="kvm", GROUP="kvm", MODE="0666", OPTIONS+="static_node=kvm"' | sudo tee /etc/udev/rules.d/99-kvm4all.rules
        sudo udevadm control --reload-rules
        sudo udevadm trigger --name-match=kvm

    - name: Assert KVM is actually usable
      run: |
        set -euo pipefail
        test -w /dev/kvm || { echo 'FATAL: /dev/kvm not writable'; ls -l /dev/kvm; exit 1; }
        echo "ok: /dev/kvm is writable"

    - name: Install QEMU
      run: |
        sudo apt-get update
        sudo apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends \
          qemu-system-x86 qemu-utils ovmf cloud-image-utils

    - uses: actions/download-artifact@v4
      with:
        name: qcow2

    - name: Seed cloud-init (SSH key for the test user)
      run: |
        set -euo pipefail
        ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -N '' -f ./id_test
        cat > user-data <<EOF
        #cloud-config
        users:
          - name: tester
            sudo: ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD:ALL
            shell: /bin/bash
            ssh_authorized_keys:
              - $(cat ./id_test.pub)
        EOF
        echo 'instance-id: ci; local-hostname: ci' > meta-data
        cloud-localds seed.iso user-data meta-data

    - name: Boot the image
      run: |
        set -euo pipefail
        qemu-system-x86_64 \
          -enable-kvm -cpu host -smp 4 -m 4096 \
          -machine q35 \
          -drive if=pflash,format=raw,readonly=on,file=/usr/share/OVMF/OVMF_CODE.fd \
          -drive file=disk.qcow2,format=qcow2,if=virtio \
          -drive file=seed.iso,format=raw,if=virtio \
          -netdev user,id=n0,hostfwd=tcp::2222-:22 -device virtio-net-pci,netdev=n0 \
          -nographic -serial file:serial.log -daemonize

    - name: Wait for SSH and verify bootc
      run: |
        set -euo pipefail
        for i in $(seq 1 60); do
          ssh -o StrictHostKeyChecking=no -o UserKnownHostsFile=/dev/null \
              -i ./id_test -p 2222 tester@127.0.0.1 true 2>/dev/null && break
          sleep 10
        done
        ssh -o StrictHostKeyChecking=no -o UserKnownHostsFile=/dev/null \
            -i ./id_test -p 2222 tester@127.0.0.1 'sudo bootc status'

    - name: Serial log (always)
      if: always()
      run: cat serial.log || true

gotchas: The udev rule must land BEFORE udev settles. A late `udevadm trigger` can leave /dev/kvm present but not writable, which fails later and looks like 'KVM not supported' rather than a permissions problem. Put the Enable-KVM step early and assert `test -w /dev/kvm` immediately after — do not let the first QEMU invocation be your probe.

`sudo usermod -aG kvm $USER` does NOT work inside a job. Supplementary group membership is resolved at login; the already-running runner shell never picks it up. The MODE="0666" udev rule is the working mechanism. Any guide recommending usermod is wrong for this context.

`cosign verify` passes on BOTH the new and legacy bundle formats, so a verify step in CI structurally cannot detect the podman/bootc invisibility regression. This is exactly how Bluefin shipped three months of silently-unsigned images. Gate on the existence of the `sha256-<digest>.sig` registry tag instead.

`--new-bundle-format` is DEPRECATED as of cosign v3.1.2 with the message 'this will be the only supported format in future versions'. It is hidden from `cosign sign --help` docs but still accepted. When cosign drops it, `--new-bundle-format=false` will start erroring or be ignored and signatures go invisible again. Pin cosign-release to an exact version and put a Renovate ignore or a review gate on that major.

Passing only `--new-bundle-format=false` is a half-fix. cosign v3.1.x also defaults `--use-signing-config` to true; both upstream bootc repos pass `--use-signing-config=false` alongside it. `--registry-referrers-mode=legacy` is a different flag (it controls fetching) and is not the fix, despite blog posts saying so.

GitHub's own runner spec table says '14 GB SSD' for ubuntu-latest, which is not the usable root filesystem. Real free space on / is ~25-29 GB before cleanup, ~51 GB after. If you plan against 14 GB you will wrongly conclude the build is impossible; if you plan against 51 GB without running a cleanup step you will hit ENOSPC mid-build.

Leave `swap-storage` / `remove-swapfile` at false in the disk-cleanup actions. Reclaiming the 4 GB swapfile means a memory-hungry bootc/osbuild step gets OOM-killed with an error that never mentions the cleanup action — a genuinely hard failure to diagnose.
The disk cleanup action mounts/removes aggressively and should run BEFORE actions/checkout (its own README says so). Running it after checkout can make the working directory inaccessible.

A fork PR's GITHUB_TOKEN is downgraded to read-only regardless of the `permissions:` block. Guard every GHCR push/sign step with the upstream `if: github.event_name != 'pull_request' && github.ref == format('refs/heads/{0}', github.event.repository.default_branch)` condition, or fork PRs fail with a 403 that reads like a permissions-block bug.

`packages: write` on GITHUB_TOKEN is enough to PUSH to GHCR but NOT enough to DELETE package versions. Pruning old image versions additionally requires granting the repository the Admin role in the package's own 'Manage Actions access' settings on ghcr.io — a per-package, manual, one-time step separate from the repo settings.

Making the GHCR package public is a manual UI step and is irreversible. Until you do it, `bootc switch` from a clean machine 401s and looks like a build failure. Also: a pushed image is not linked to its repository by default, so it will not inherit repo visibility — set `org.opencontainers.image.source` (as ublue does) to get the link.

A nightly build workflow does not reset its own 60-day inactivity timer, because workflow runs are not repository activity — only new commits are. A stable repo with a green nightly build will go quiet and then silently stop building. Add a keepalive or an external cron calling workflow_dispatch.

`ubuntu-latest` migrates from 24.04 to 26.04 between 2026-10-19 and 2026-11-19, rolled out gradually. A nightly build on `ubuntu-latest` will get a mix of both images during that window. Pin the version explicitly; ublue-os/image-template has already moved to `ubuntu-26.04`.

Keyless cosign verification on the CONSUMER side is the untested half. Both production bootc repos examined (ublue-os/image-template, Danathar/arch-bootc) use KEY-based signing with a static cosign.pub, because the bootc/ostree `containers-policy.json` path is well-trodden for `sigstoreSigned` + `keyPath`. Keyless requires a fulcio CA cert + rekor public key + a signedIdentity/certificate-identity match in policy.json. I did not find a primary source demonstrating this working end-to-end for bootc. Prototype the consumer-side policy BEFORE committing to keyless.

Splitting build (no KVM, privileged podman) from VM-test (KVM, no privileged podman) keeps the KVM dependency off the publishing critical path. If /dev/kvm availability regresses on hosted runners, you lose testing but not releases.

The Fedora KDE bootc reference image (ublue-os/aurora) has 256 layers. Layer-count-sensitive tooling and slow registry round-trips are real; consider rechunking (`rpm-ostree` rechunk or coreos/chunkah, both wired into ublue-os/image-template) to cut delta-update size and layer churn.
blockers: PREMISE CONTRADICTION (question 5): a workflow in repo A CANNOT trigger repo B via repository_dispatch with the default GITHUB_TOKEN. Note the reason is not the one usually cited — the docs explicitly exempt repository_dispatch and workflow_dispatch from the GITHUB_TOKEN recursion-prevention rule ('repository_dispatch events always create workflow runs'). The actual blocker is scope: GITHUB_TOKEN is issued for the repository containing the workflow and cannot authenticate POST /repos/{other}/{repo}/dispatches. You must supply a PAT (classic: `repo` scope) or, preferably, a GitHub App installation token scoped to repo B with Contents: write. Budget a secret and an App installation.

PREMISE CORRECTION (question 2): disk space is NOT a hard blocker, contrary to the framing. Upstream osbuild's own CI builds raw+qcow2+vmdk+vhd from a Fedora image on a free ubuntu-24.04 runner inside 45 minutes with a single cleanup step. The Fedora KDE bootc reference image is 3.71 GB compressed (~9-11 GB unpacked), and post-cleanup free space is ~51 GB. It fits — but ONLY with a cleanup step; the ~25-29 GB baseline is not enough for image + qcow2 together, so treat the cleanup step as a hard dependency rather than an optimization.

NOT BLOCKING BUT TIME-BOXED: the `--new-bundle-format=false` workaround is explicitly deprecated upstream ('this will be the only supported format in future versions'), while containers/container-libs#388 — the issue that would let podman/bootc read the new format — has been OPEN since 2025-10-12 with no fix. If cosign removes the flag before containers/image gains referrer support, keyless-or-keyed signing for bootc consumers breaks with no workaround. Pin cosign to an exact version, and track containers/container-libs#388 as a project risk rather than assuming it resolves.

That older function is now simply a wrapper for SHGetKnownFolderPath." / "The calling process is responsible for freeing this resource ... by calling CoTaskMemFree"

facts.claim: The KNOWNFOLDERID GUIDs needed are: Desktop {B4BFCC3A-DB2C-424C-B029-7FE99A87C641}, Documents {FDD39AD0-238F-46AF-ADB4-6C85480369C7}, Downloads {374DE290-123F-4565-9164-39C4925E467B}, Pictures {33E28130-4E1E-4676-835A-98395C3BC3BB}, Music {4BD8D571-6D19-48D3-BE97-422220080E43}, Videos {18989B1D-99B5-455B-841C-AB7C74E4DDFC}, Profile {5E6C858F-0E22-4760-9AFE-EA3317B67173}, RoamingAppData {3EB685DB-65F9-4CF6-A03A-E3EF65729F3D}, LocalAppData {F1B32785-6FBA-4FCF-9D55-7B8E7F157091}, SkyDrive {A52BBA46-E9E1-435f-B3D9-28DAA648C0F6}.
