# Or, to reapply the whole Global Theme (appearance + layout) for the current user:
plasma-apply-lookandfeel -a com.example.winlike.desktop

# Nuclear reset so the first-run layout script runs again at next login:
#   rm ~/.config/plasma-org.kde.plasma.desktop-appletsrc && kquitapp6 plasmashell && plasmashell &

gotchas: `plasma-apply-layoutscript` is not a real command. It appears in no KDE repo, on no branch, and in no shipped package. Anything in the plan that depends on it has to be rewritten.

`/etc/xdg/plasma-org.kde.plasma.desktop-appletsrc` is silently ignored. libplasma opens the containment config with KConfig::SimpleConfig, which disables the XDG cascade entirely. You get no error - you just get the stock Breeze panel.

The Global Theme's `contents/defaults` beats `/etc/xdg/kdeglobals`. startplasma prepends `~/.config/kdedefaults` to XDG_CONFIG_DIRS and writes the active look-and-feel's defaults there at every session start. Appearance keys you set in /etc/xdg/kdeglobals will be overwritten unless you mark them `[$i]` or move them into your own LnF package.

Plasma 6 already defaults to double-click (`SingleClick=false`). Do not 'fix' a problem that does not exist; the real Windows-parity gap in the same group is `DndBehavior` (KDE asks on every intra-drive drag; Windows just moves).
`logout` needs two keys: `logout=false` AND `action/logout=false`. KDE checks `authorizeAction("logout")` and `authorize("logout")` and both must pass. Setting only one leaves logout available.
Control-module restrictions go in `/etc/kde5rc`, not `/etc/kde6rc`. KConfig in Frameworks 6 still hardcodes the KF5-era filename.

Half the keys on develop.kde.org's Kiosk page are KDE 3/4 leftovers aimed at konqiconviewrc and konsolerc. Only the subset listed as verified above is provably still read by Plasma 6 code. Test the rest before promising it to a customer.

Discover has no backend on/off switch. If someone proposes a `discoverrc` key for it, it does not exist - the only options are not installing the plugin, deleting the .so, or `--backends` on the Exec line.
`plasma-discover-rpm-ostree` arrives via a weak dependency on Kinoite-like bases (`Supplements: ((plasma-discover and rpm-ostree) unless dnf)`), so it is installed unless you explicitly remove it.

If you strip every non-Flatpak Discover backend, users lose the only GUI path to OS updates. On bootc the OS updates itself via bootc-fetch-apply-updates.timer, so this may be fine - but the welcome app should say so, because Discover will now report 'up to date' while knowing nothing about the base image.

Flatpaks cannot be baked into a bootc image. System flatpaks live in /var/lib/flatpak, and bootc treats image /var as a Docker VOLUME: unpacked from the initial image only, never updated. Use `/usr/share/flatpak/preinstall.d/` + `flatpak preinstall`, not a pre-populated /var.
`remotes.d` only auto-applies to the DEFAULT system installation. It is skipped for `--user` installs and for extra installations defined in /etc/flatpak/installations.d/.

`/etc/skel` is a one-shot at account creation. Shipping a new taskbar in /etc/skel in image v2 does nothing for users created under v1. The look-and-feel layout script has the same limitation (it only runs for users with no containments), so plan a versioned migration path from day one - e.g. a per-user systemd user unit that compares a stamp and calls plasma-apply-lookandfeel.

xdg-user-dirs translates folder names into the user's locale. 'Documents' becomes 'Documenti' in Italian. Windows does the same thing at the display layer, so this is probably desirable - but if your support docs say 'open Documents', they will be wrong for non-English users.
Dolphin's default view mode lives in `~/.local/share/dolphin/view_properties/global/.directory`, not in dolphinrc, so it cannot be set from /etc/xdg at all.

Windows-like global themes are all third-party and unvetted. Nothing in Fedora repos gets you Win11 chrome. Shipping Windows-lookalike icon/decoration artwork in a commercial product is a trademark and trade-dress exposure - get that reviewed before it lands in an image.
`/etc/xdg/plasma-workspace/env/*.sh` is for environment variables only. It runs before the window manager; do not put config-seeding or GUI commands there.
blockers: Requirement 1 names `plasma-apply-layoutscript`. That binary does not exist in Plasma 5 or Plasma 6 - verified by recursive git-tree search of KDE/plasma-workspace (master and Plasma/5.27) and by the shipped file list of plasma-workspace 6.7.5. The requirement must be restated in terms of the Look-and-Feel package's contents/layouts/org.kde.plasma.desktop-layout.js (first-run) plus org.kde.PlasmaShell.evaluateScript over D-Bus (runtime).

Requirement 1 also names `/etc/xdg/plasma-org.kde.plasma.desktop-appletsrc` as a system-wide default. This cannot work: libplasma opens that file with KConfig::SimpleConfig, which bypasses the XDG cascade. Shipping a system-wide literal appletsrc is only possible via /etc/skel, which does not propagate to existing users on image update.

Requirement 3's premise is factually wrong for the target. Plasma 6's `kdeglobals [KDE] SingleClick` default is already `false` - double-click to open, single-click to select, i.e. Windows behaviour - per plasma-desktop's workspaceoptions_kdeglobalssettings.kcfg. There is nothing to change.

Requirement 5 asks how to DISABLE the rpm/dnf backend in Discover via configuration. No such configuration exists - DiscoverBackendsFactory enumerates plugin .so files on disk and the only override is the `--backends` command-line option. This has to be solved at package/image-build level, not in a config file.

Requirement 5 also implicitly assumes flatpaks can be preconfigured in the image. On bootc they cannot be pre-installed: /var/lib/flatpak follows Docker VOLUME semantics and is only ever unpacked from the initial image. First-boot install via `flatpak preinstall` is unavoidable, which means the 'zero-terminal' promise depends on network at first boot.

Requirement 2 has no shippable answer today. There is no Windows-like Global Theme in Fedora's repositories, and the third-party candidates (KDE Store 'Windows Eleven Plasma 6', doncsugar/willow-theme) are unpackaged, of uncertain Plasma 6 status, and carry trade-dress risk. Building our own look-and-feel package is cheap and is the only defensible path; budget for it rather than treating it as a download.

area: Running Windows .exe programs on a Fedora KDE atomic/bootc desktop (Bottles/WINE vs. Windows-in-a-container), as of 2026-09-20

facts.claim: Bottles is officially distributed ONLY as a Flatpak, which makes it a natural fit for an immutable/bootc host — no rpm-ostree layering needed. Upstream says so explicitly.
facts.evidence: https://docs.usebottles.com/getting-started/installation — "We currently only offer Bottles as a flatpak package"; "The Flatpak package is the only fully sandboxed version. It bundles all the needed dependencies and tools". README (https://github.com/bottlesdevs/Bottles) lists only Flathub + cpak as install channels.
facts.impact: Our bootc image does not need Wine, winetricks, or 32-bit libs layered into /usr. Bottles ships its own Wine base (base: org.winehq.Wine, base-version: stable-25.08). Image stays clean.

facts.claim: The Flathub Bottles manifest grants NO access to the user's home directory. There is no --filesystem=home and no --filesystem=host. File access outside the sandbox goes through portals (libportal is built into the app).
facts.evidence: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/flathub/com.usebottles.bottles/master/com.usebottles.bottles.yml — finish-args are exactly: --allow=devel, --allow=multiarch, --allow=per-app-dev-shm, --share=network, --share=ipc, --socket=x11, --socket=wayland, --socket=pulseaudio, --device=all, --filesystem=xdg-data/umu:create, --filesystem=~/Games/umu:create, --system-talk-name=org.freedesktop.UDisks2, plus env/PATH. Module list includes 'libportal'.
facts.impact: Out of the box a user CANNOT double-click an .exe sitting in ~/Downloads and have it work with its sibling data files. Our first-run provisioning must either (a) run `flatpak override --user --filesystem=<dir>` for a designated app directory, or (b) instruct users to copy installers into the bottle. This is a real support-ticket generator and must be in the deployment script, not left to the user.

facts.claim: Bottles' own docs confirm the sandboxed Wine userdir: since Bottles 2021.10.14, the Windows Desktop/Documents/Downloads folders inside a bottle are plain directories, NOT symlinks to the real $HOME. Exposing the real home is explicitly discouraged by upstream.
facts.evidence: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/bottlesdevs/documentation/master/flatpak/expose-directories/use-system-home.md — "Starting from Bottles 2021.10.14, the userdir path is sandboxed, so the above symlinks don't exist." and "this is a practice discouraged by Bottles and we take no responsibility for what may happen after exposing your homedir to the runner".
facts.impact: A teacher saving a Word file from a Wine app will save it INSIDE the bottle, not in their Documents folder, unless we wire this up. We must either script the symlink relink (upstream-discouraged) or train users to use the portal file chooser.

facts.claim: Bottles is Flathub-verified and GPL-3.0-only, so it should survive Fedora's planned 'Flathub verified FLOSS subset' filter on Atomic Desktops.
facts.evidence: https://flathub.org/api/v2/verification/com.usebottles.bottles/status → {"verified":true,"timestamp":"1675731252","method":"website","website":"usebottles.com"}; https://flathub.org/api/v2/appstream/com.usebottles.bottles → project_license: GPL-3.0-only.
facts.impact: Safe to depend on Flathub for Bottles on Fedora Atomic. But see the Flathub-remote gotcha: on stock Fedora Kinoite today Flathub is not unconditionally enabled, so our image must add the remote itself.

facts.claim: Fedora's change to enable a filtered 'Flathub verified FLOSS subset' by default on Atomic Desktops is accepted for Fedora 45, i.e. it is NOT the current behaviour on shipping Fedora 42/43/44 Kinoite.
facts.evidence: https://fedoraproject.org/wiki/Changes/FilterFedoraFlatpaksAtomicDesktopsv2 — categorized ChangeAcceptedF45, described as "a second attempt at this Change proposal after being rejected in the F43 cycle"; Flathub's own Fedora page (https://flathub.org/en/setup/Fedora) still tells users to enable Flathub via Third-Party Repositories or `flatpak remote-add --if-not-exists flathub https://dl.flathub.org/repo/flathub.flatpakrepo`.
facts.impact: Our bootc image must ship the Flathub remote definition itself (in /usr, not /var) rather than assuming Fedora provides it.

facts.claim: In bootc, content in /var from the container image is unpacked ONLY from the initial image and is never updated by subsequent image updates. /var/lib/flatpak (system Flatpak installation) lives in /var.
facts.evidence: https://bootc.dev/bootc/filesystem.html — "content included in /var in the container image acts like a Docker VOLUME /var. This means its contents are unpacked _only from the initial image_ - subsequent changes to /var in a container image are not automatically applied."
facts.impact: Do NOT `flatpak install --system` during the image build expecting it to update with the image. Anything baked into /var/lib/flatpak freezes at install time. Use the preinstall.d mechanism in /usr instead (next fact).

facts.claim: The correct, upstream-supported mechanism to declare 'these Flatpaks are part of the OS' from an OCI image is a .preinstall drop-in in /usr/share/flatpak/preinstall.d/ plus `flatpak preinstall -y` at boot. /usr IS lifecycled with the bootc image.
facts.evidence: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/flatpak/flatpak/main/doc/flatpak-preinstall.xml — "Preinstalled flatpaks are defined by dropping .preinstall files into the directories /usr/share/flatpak/preinstall.d/ and /etc/flatpak/preinstall.d/. The OS runs flatpak preinstall -y (or its GUI equivalent) on system startup, which then does the actual installation." and "Users can opt out of preinstalled flatpaks by simply uninstalling them, at which point they won't get automatically reinstalled again." Universal Blue ships a flatpak-preinstall.service for exactly this.
facts.impact: This is the mechanism for shipping Bottles (and Flatseal) in our image. It is declarative, updatable with the image, and user-overridable. Put the .preinstall file in /usr/share/flatpak/preinstall.d/.

facts.claim: A Bottles prefix CANNOT be baked into the OCI image. Bottles stores everything under $XDG_DATA_HOME/bottles, which inside the Flatpak resolves to ~/.var/app/com.usebottles.bottles/data/bottles — per-user, in $HOME, which no OS image controls.
facts.evidence: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/bottlesdevs/Bottles/main/bottles/backend/globals.py — `xdg_data_home = os.environ.get("XDG_DATA_HOME", os.path.join(Path.home(), ".local/share"))`; `base = _get_wine_compatible_base(f"{xdg_data_home}/bottles")`; `bottles = f"{base}/bottles"`, `runners = f"{base}/runners"`. Bottles docs confirm the path `~/.var/app/com.usebottles.bottles/data/bottles/bottles`.
facts.impact: Answers Q3 directly and negatively. Our provisioning must be: bake a TEMPLATE prefix tarball into /usr/share/<ourorg>/, then a per-user first-run unit copies/extracts it into ~/.var/app/com.usebottles.bottles/data/bottles/bottles/<name>. Budget disk: a prefix plus runner is hundreds of MB per user.

facts.claim: Copying a fully-provisioned Wine prefix per user is the upstream-sanctioned approach; sharing one prefix between users is explicitly NOT supported.
facts.evidence: Wine FAQ (https://gitlab.winehq.org/wine/wine/-/wikis/FAQ), 'Can I install applications to be shared by multiple users?' — "Wine does not currently allow sharing its configuration (\"prefixes\") between users, due to the risk of registry corruption from running multiple wineservers simultaneously (bug #11112). At present, applications must be installed separately for each user. However, you can copy Wine prefixes; you can install everything to one prefix, then make a copy of it in each user's home directory. This saves running installers repeatedly."
facts.impact: Validates the template-copy design. Rules out a shared /usr/share prefix or an NFS-mounted one. Also rules out any 'install once for the whole lab' claim.

facts.claim: Bottles has a real CLI (bottles-cli) capable of headless bottle creation, program registration, registry edits and running executables — so first-run provisioning can be fully scripted.
facts.evidence: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/bottlesdevs/Bottles/main/bottles/frontend/cli/cli.py — subcommands: info, list, programs, add, tools, reg, reg-rules, edit, new, run, autostart, stop, standalone, shell, umu. `new` takes --bottle-name (required), --environment (gaming|application|custom, required), --custom-environment, --arch, --runner, --dxvk, --vkd3d, --nvapi, --latencyflex. There is also an `autostart` subcommand ("Run programs configured to start at login") and `standalone` ("Generate a standalone script to launch commands without passing trough Bottles").
facts.impact: First-run provisioning is a shell script invoking `flatpak run --command=bottles-cli com.usebottles.bottles ...`, driven by a systemd --user oneshot with a stamp file. No GUI clicking required.

facts.claim: WineHQ AppDB rating definitions, verbatim — these are the words we must use honestly on a website.
facts.evidence: https://gitlab.winehq.org/winehq/appdb/-/wikis/Rating-Definitions — Platinum: "Works as well as (or better than) on Windows out of the box." Gold: "Works as well as (or better than) on Windows with workarounds." Silver: "Works excellently for normal use, but has some problems for which there are no workarounds." Bronze: "Works, but has some problems for normal use." Garbage: "Problems are severe enough that it cannot be used for the purpose it was designed for."
facts.impact: Note that even GOLD means 'with workarounds' and SILVER means 'has problems with no workarounds'. Citing 'Gold on WineHQ' as 'works' is already a stretch for a non-technical buyer.

facts.claim: Microsoft Office: modern versions are rated Garbage on WineHQ AppDB. Only pre-2016 versions are good.
facts.evidence: https://appdb.winehq.org/objectManager.php?sClass=application&iId=31 ('Microsoft Office (installer only)'), read 2026-09-20: 2003 Platinum, 2007 Platinum (98 results), 2010 32-bit Gold, 2010 64-bit Garbage, 2013 32-bit Silver, 2016 32-bit Silver (tested Wine 9.3), 2016 64-bit Bronze, 2019 (HUP) Silver, 2021 Pro Plus **Garbage** (Wine 9.0), 365 Business **Garbage** (Wine 11.0), 365 ProPlus (2016) **Garbage** (Wine 7.2, 56 comments).
facts.impact: We must never say 'Office works'. The honest line for a school is: Office 2007/2010 may run; Office 2021 and Microsoft 365 do not. Steer to LibreOffice + Office on the web.

facts.claim: Adobe Photoshop: every Creative Cloud release from CC 2019 through CC 2024 is only Silver, several on very old Wine versions with 2-8 test results. There is no AppDB entry at all for Photoshop 2025/2026.
facts.evidence: https://appdb.winehq.org/objectManager.php?sClass=application&iId=17 read 2026-09-20: 7.0 Gold; CS Platinum; CS3 Platinum; CS4 Bronze; CS6 Silver (Wine 11.0); CC 2018 Bronze; CC 2019 Silver; CC 2020 Silver; CC 2021 Silver; CC 2022 Silver (3 results); CC 2023 Silver (5 results); CC 2024 Silver (Wine 9.15-staging, 2 test results). Newest list entry is CC 2024.
facts.impact: Adobe is a hard no for us. Silver literally means "has some problems for which there are no workarounds", the sample sizes are tiny, and the Creative Cloud installer/licensing layer is the part that actually fails. Do not list Adobe as supported at any tier.

facts.claim: .NET is version-dependent and non-monotonic: .NET Framework 2.0/3.5/4.8 are Platinum, but 4.5/4.6/4.6.2/4.7/4.7.1 are Silver, 1.1 is Garbage, and 4.8.1 is Garbage on Wine 11.10.
facts.evidence: https://appdb.winehq.org/objectManager.php?sClass=application&iId=2586 read 2026-09-20: 1.0 Gold, 1.1 Garbage, 2.0 Platinum, 3.0 Gold, 3.5 Platinum, 4.0 Gold, 4.5 Silver, 4.5.2 Gold, 4.6 Silver, 4.6.1 Gold, 4.6.2 Silver, 4.7 Silver, 4.7.1 Silver, 4.8 Platinum (Wine 10.12), 4.8.1 Garbage (Wine 11.10).
facts.impact: A customer's line-of-business .NET app is a coin flip decided by which Framework version its installer demands. We can honestly say 'many .NET Framework 4.8 apps run' and must test per app. Wine also ships wine-mono, which upstream says "For many .NET apps, particularly older ones, this is sufficient".

facts.claim: Wine cannot install or run Windows kernel drivers, full stop. This is the structural reason printer/scanner vendor utilities, HASP/Sentinel/CodeMeter dongles, and kernel anti-cheat will never work under Bottles.
facts.evidence: Wine FAQ (https://gitlab.winehq.org/wine/wine/-/wikis/FAQ): "Can I use Wine to install drivers for my hardware? No. Wine requires your hardware to already be working on your operating system. The technical reason for this is that Wine, like most applications, runs in user mode and not kernel mode."
facts.impact: Category-level exclusion we can state with confidence and without hedging: anything that ships a .sys driver is out. Printers/scanners must work via the Linux CUPS/SANE driver instead; the Windows vendor utility will not.

facts.claim: Wine provides NO security isolation. A Windows app under Wine can do anything the user can. The Flatpak sandbox is the only boundary, and Bottles' manifest already weakens it with --allow=devel (ptrace/perf_event_open) and --device=all.
facts.evidence: Wine FAQ: "Wine does not sandbox in any way at all. When run under Wine, a Windows app can do anything your user can. Wine does not (and cannot) stop a Windows app directly making native syscalls, messing with your files, altering your startup scripts, or doing other nasty things. You need to use AppArmor, SELinux or some type of virtual machine if you want to properly sandbox Windows apps." flatpak-build-finish(1) (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/flatpak/flatpak/main/doc/flatpak-build-finish.xml): "The devel feature allows the application to access certain syscalls such as ptrace(), and perf_event_open()." "The multiarch feature allows the application to execute programs compiled for an ABI other than the one supported natively by the system." Flatpak docs: --device=all = "All devices, including all of the above except shm".
facts.impact: If we ever pitch this to a school, the security story is 'Flatpak sandbox minus devel and device=all', not 'Wine is safe'. Do not claim isolation. Keeping the default no-home-access permission set is actually our strongest safety argument — do not blanket-grant --filesystem=home.

facts.claim: Kernel-level anti-cheat does not work under Wine/Proton AND does not work in a Windows VM either, because those anti-cheats detect and block virtualization.
facts.evidence: winapps README (https://github.com/winapps-org/winapps): "Support does not, however, extend to kernel-level anti-cheat systems (e.g. Riot Vanguard)". WinBoat FAQ (https://winboat.app/): "Does it run games with anti-cheat that don't run on Linux? Unfortunately running games with kernel anti-cheat is not possible, as they block virtualization." EAC and BattlEye have shipped opt-in Proton-compatible runtimes since 2022, but enabling them is the game developer's choice.
facts.impact: There is no escape hatch for Vanguard/Ricochet-class titles. Both our WINE path and our VM path fail. State it plainly.

facts.claim: WinApps exists, is actively maintained, and works by running a real Windows VM (dockur/windows) and projecting individual windows via FreeRDP RemoteApp. Its shipped compose file requests 4 GB RAM and 4 CPU cores for the VM, plus 64 GB disk.
facts.evidence: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/winapps-org/winapps/main/compose.yaml — image ghcr.io/dockur/windows:latest, VERSION: "11", RAM_SIZE: "4G", CPU_CORES: "4", DISK_SIZE: "64G", devices /dev/kvm and /dev/net/tun, ports 127.0.0.1:3389, volume ./oem:/oem "applying Windows registry modifications contained within 'oem/RDPApps.reg'". README: "Using FreeRDP as a backend to seamlessly render Windows applications alongside GNU/Linux applications" and "The GNU/Linux /home directory is accessible within Windows via the \\tsclient\home mount."
facts.impact: This is the only path that actually runs Office/Adobe correctly — because it IS Windows. But the resource cost is a whole second OS. On a 4 GB 2012 laptop this is not deployable.

facts.claim: The Windows image WinApps/WinBoat use defaults to Windows 11 Pro and the project explicitly disclaims licensing: you must bring your own valid Windows license.
facts.evidence: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/dockur/windows/master/readme.md — "By default, Windows 11 Pro will be installed." Version table: 11=Windows 11 Pro, 11l=11 LTSC, 11e=11 Enterprise, 10=Windows 10 Pro, 10l=10 LTSC, etc. "Yes, this project contains only open-source code and does not distribute Windows itself. Any product keys found in the code are generic installation keys published by Microsoft for trial purposes and are not valid activation licenses. You are responsible for ensuring that you have a valid Windows license and that your use complies with Microsoft's licensing terms." Requirements: "Docker or Podman on a Linux host with KVM support", "At least 2 GB of available RAM", "At least 32 GB of free disk space". WinBoat FAQ: "WinBoat does not provide any licenses for Windows. All the default ISO-s WinBoat downloads ship with the trial version of the operating system... and you must bring your own license key to activate it."
facts.impact: Pro (not Home) is required because Home has no RDP server. For a school this means a per-device Windows Pro license on top of the Linux migration — which defeats the stated purpose of the migration. Must be said out loud in any proposal.

facts.claim: WinBoat is real, MIT-licensed, and at v0.8.0 is self-described as BETA. It has no GPU acceleration, and its Podman support (needed on Fedora Atomic, which ships Podman not Docker) arrived in v0.9.0 without USB passthrough.
facts.evidence: https://winboat.app/ read 2026-09-20 — "Current version: v0.8.0"; "🚧 WinBoat is currently in Beta, so expect to occasionally run into hiccups and bugs. You should be comfortable with some level of troubleshooting"; hardware prereqs "RAM: At least 4 GB of RAM", "CPU: At least 2 CPU threads", "Storage: At least 32 GB of free space", "Virtualization: KVM enabled in BIOS/UEFI", "FreeRDP ... Version 3.x.x with sound support"; "Docker Desktop is not supported"; FAQ "Is there GPU acceleration/passthrough? Not at the moment"; "Podman is now supported starting from WinBoat v0.9.0 ... USB passthrough via Podman is not supported yet"; "Will you publish WinBoat as a Flatpak? This is on our to-do list".
facts.impact: On a bootc host there is no Docker and no easy way to add one; WinBoat is distributed as AppImage/deb/rpm, not Flatpak, so it does not install cleanly on an atomic desktop without layering. Combined with 'Beta' this is not something to sell to a school.

facts.claim: ProtonDB has a working public JSON endpoint keyed by Steam AppID — this is the ONLY machine-readable compatibility source I could actually query, and it only covers Steam games.
facts.evidence: I ran: curl -s https://www.protondb.com/api/v1/reports/summaries/570.json → HTTP 200, body {"bestReportedTier":"platinum","confidence":"strong","score":0.69,"tier":"gold","total":356,"trendingTier":"gold"}. A nonexistent id (0) returns 404. It is undocumented/unofficial — no rate-limit or stability guarantee is published.
facts.impact: Useful for a game-focused checker, useless for a customer's list of business .exe files. Do not build the customer-facing 'will my app work' feature on this alone.

facts.claim: Two other queryable datasets exist and work: AreWeAntiCheatYet (a plain games.json in git) and the Lutris games API (which covers non-game Windows apps and tells you whether an install script exists).
facts.evidence: curl https://raw.githubusercontent.com/AreWeAntiCheatYet/AreWeAntiCheatYet/HEAD/games.json → HTTP 200, array of {name, status, anticheats[], notes[]}. curl 'https://lutris.net/api/games?search=photoshop' → HTTP 200, {"count":4,...} including "Adobe Photoshop 2019", "Adobe Photoshop CC" with platforms:[{"name":"Windows"}].
facts.impact: A realistic 'app intake' checker = Lutris API (does a community install recipe exist?) + ProtonDB (games) + AreWeAntiCheatYet (anti-cheat) + our own hand-curated table for business software. The curated table will do most of the work.

facts.claim: The current Wine series is 11.x — AppDB's 'Wine version tested' dropdown tops out at 11.18 as of 2026-09-20.
facts.evidence: https://appdb.winehq.org (Browse Applications filter form) version list read 2026-09-20: 11.18, 11.17, ... 11.0, 11.0-rc5 ... 10.20, 10.19, 10.18. AppDB reports 16,629 application entries.
facts.impact: Lets us say 'tested against Wine 11.x' honestly, and lets us spot stale AppDB ratings (e.g. Photoshop CC 2024's Silver was tested on Wine 9.15-staging — two years stale, 2 reports).

facts.claim: CodeWeavers, the commercial Wine vendor, appears to have dropped Microsoft Office 365 from CrossOver's supported list as of mid-2026.
facts.evidence: Search result snippets for https://www.codeweavers.com/compatibility/crossover/microsoft-office-365 state Office 365 is "no longer supported on CrossOver", updated June 16, 2026, and a forum thread titled "No longer supporting Microsoft Office…". I could NOT read the page directly: codeweavers.com returns HTTP 403 behind a Cloudflare JS challenge to both curl and WebFetch.
facts.impact: Strong supporting argument that Office-on-Wine is a dead end, but it is snippet-level evidence. Do not quote a date or exact wording on a customer-facing page without re-verifying from a browser.

snippets.name: Bottles Flathub finish-args (verbatim, com.usebottles.bottles.yml, master, read 2026-09-20) — note: NO home/host filesystem access

sdk: org.gnome.Sdk
runtime: org.gnome.Platform
base: org.winehq.Wine
base-version: stable-25.08
runtime-version: '50'
command: bottles

finish-args:
  - --allow=devel
  - --allow=multiarch
  - --allow=per-app-dev-shm
  - --share=network

snippets.name: flatpak preinstall mechanism (verbatim from flatpak-preinstall(1))
snippets.code:
Preinstalled flatpaks are defined by dropping .preinstall files into the directories /usr/share/flatpak/preinstall.d/ and /etc/flatpak/preinstall.d/. The OS runs flatpak preinstall -y (or its GUI equivalent) on system startup, which then does the actual installation.

This system allows the OS vendor to define the list of flatpaks that are installed together with the OS, and also makes it possible for the OS vendor to make changes to the list in the future, which is then applied once flatpak preinstall is run next time.

Users can opt out of preinstalled flatpaks by simply uninstalling them, at which point they won't get automatically reinstalled again.

set -euo pipefail

BOTTLES_DATA="$HOME/.var/app/com.usebottles.bottles/data/bottles"
STAMP="$HOME/.local/state/ourorg/bottle-seeded"

mkdir -p "$BOTTLES_DATA/bottles" "$(dirname "$STAMP")"

    -C "$BOTTLES_DATA/bottles"

  add --bottle "SchoolApps" \
      --name "Legacy LOB App" \

snippets.name: Wine FAQ, verbatim — the two answers that decide most of our scope
snippets.code:
Can I use Wine to install drivers for my hardware?

No. Wine requires your hardware to already be working on your operating system. The technical reason for this is that Wine, like most applications, runs in user mode and not kernel mode.

---

How good is Wine at sandboxing Windows apps?

Wine does not sandbox in any way at all. When run under Wine, a Windows app can do anything your user can. Wine does not (and cannot) stop a Windows app directly making native syscalls, messing with your files, altering your startup scripts, or doing other nasty things.

You need to use AppArmor, SELinux or some type of virtual machine if you want to properly sandbox Windows apps.

snippets.name: Wine FAQ, verbatim — why prefixes must be copied per user (this is our Q3 answer)
snippets.code:
Can I install applications to be shared by multiple users?

Wine does not currently allow sharing its configuration ("prefixes") between users, due to the risk of registry corruption from running multiple wineservers simultaneously (bug #11112). At present, applications must be installed separately for each user.

However, you can copy Wine prefixes; you can install everything to one prefix, then make a copy of it in each user's home directory. This saves running installers repeatedly.

snippets.name: Honest one-sentence website claims (drafted; pick one)
snippets.code:
PREFERRED (specific, falsifiable, no promise):
"Some Windows programs run on our desktops through Bottles/WINE — we check each one on your list against the WineHQ Application Database before we quote, and we tell you which ones will not run."

ALTERNATIVE (leads with the exclusion):
"We do not claim Windows compatibility: we test your actual .exe list first and give you a per-app verdict — works, works with caveats, or does not work — before anything is migrated."

DO NOT WRITE:
"Runs your Windows apps." / "Full .exe support." / "Office and Adobe work through WINE."

gotchas: Bottles on Flathub has NO home directory access by default. There is no --filesystem=home in the manifest. A user double-clicking an .exe in ~/Downloads will hit a wall, and the app will not see its sibling DLLs/data files. This is the single most likely support ticket. Budget for it in the provisioning script (`flatpak override --user --filesystem=<dir>`), and ship Flatseal.

Bottles sandboxes the Wine userdir since 2021.10.14 — Desktop/Documents/Downloads inside the bottle are NOT symlinks to the real home. Files a user 'saves to Documents' from a Windows app land inside the bottle where they will never find them. Upstream explicitly discourages the symlink workaround: "we take no responsibility for what may happen after exposing your homedir to the runner".

Do not `flatpak install --system` during the bootc image build. /var/lib/flatpak is in /var, and bootc unpacks image /var content only at initial install — it is never refreshed by later image updates. Use /usr/share/flatpak/preinstall.d/ + `flatpak preinstall -y` at boot instead.

Flathub is not guaranteed to be enabled on stock Fedora Kinoite today. The 'Flathub verified FLOSS subset by default' change is ChangeAcceptedF45, i.e. it lands with Fedora 45, not before. Our image must ship the remote definition.

'Gold' on WineHQ does not mean 'works'. It means "Works as well as (or better than) on Windows with workarounds." 'Silver' means "has some problems for which there are no workarounds." Citing a Gold rating as 'supported' in a sales context is already shading the truth.

AppDB ratings are frequently stale and low-N. Photoshop CC 2024's Silver was recorded on Wine 9.15-staging with 2 test results; the current Wine series is 11.18. Always read the 'Latest Wine version tested' and 'Test results' columns, not just the colour.

The whole Office family above 2016 is Garbage-rated, including '365 Business' (tested on Wine 11.0, i.e. recent). Office 2021 Pro Plus is Garbage. Modern Office uses the Click-to-Run installer, which is the part that fails.

Anything shipping a Windows kernel driver (.sys) is categorically out under WINE: HASP/Sentinel/CodeMeter dongles, most printer/scanner vendor utilities, TWAIN drivers, and kernel anti-cheat. Bottles' --device=all exposes the Linux device nodes, which does NOT help — Wine still cannot load the Windows driver that talks to them.

Kernel anti-cheat also fails in the VM route, not just WINE: WinBoat's own FAQ says "running games with kernel anti-cheat is not possible, as they block virtualization." There is no configuration that fixes this.

WinApps/WinBoat need Windows Pro or better (Home has no RDP server; dockur defaults to Windows 11 Pro) AND a real Windows license the customer must supply. Selling a Linux migration that requires buying Windows Pro per device is close to self-refuting — say so before the customer discovers it.

WinBoat is self-declared BETA at v0.8.0 ("expect to occasionally run into hiccups and bugs. You should be comfortable with some level of troubleshooting"), has no GPU acceleration, is not packaged as a Flatpak, and only gained Podman support in v0.9.0 (without USB passthrough). On a bootc host there is no Docker, so this is layering or nothing.

WineHQ AppDB is behind an Anubis proof-of-work challenge as of 2026-09-20 — I confirmed curl and WebFetch both get the challenge page. Any 'automatically check the customer's app list against AppDB' feature will either break or amount to working around a deliberate anti-scraping measure. Plan on a hand-curated internal table plus manual AppDB lookups instead.

ProtonDB's JSON endpoint is undocumented and unofficial with no published stability or rate-limit guarantees, and it is keyed by Steam AppID — it cannot answer anything about a school's line-of-business .exe.

Wine provides zero security isolation. Only the Flatpak sandbox does, and Bottles' manifest already grants --allow=devel (ptrace, perf_event_open) and --device=all. Do not describe this setup as 'sandboxed Windows apps' without that qualification.
blockers: Q3's premise is wrong as stated: a Bottles prefix CANNOT be pre-configured inside the OCI image. Bottles stores prefixes under $XDG_DATA_HOME/bottles, which in the Flatpak is ~/.var/app/com.usebottles.bottles/data/bottles — per-user, in $HOME, which no bootc image controls. The image can only ship (a) the Bottles Flatpak via /usr/share/flatpak/preinstall.d/ and (b) a template prefix tarball in /usr. It MUST be materialised per user at first run, via a systemd --user oneshot with a stamp file. Wine upstream independently confirms the copy-per-user model is the only supported one ("applications must be installed separately for each user... you can copy Wine prefixes").

Q5's premise is largely wrong: there is no WineHQ AppDB API. The AppDB is a PHP/MySQL web app (per its own README) with no JSON endpoint, and as of 2026-09-20 it is gated by an Anubis proof-of-work challenge that blocks plain HTTP clients. Building a customer-facing 'paste your app list and we'll check it' feature against AppDB is not achievable without circumventing a deliberate anti-bot control. What IS queryable: ProtonDB's unofficial summaries JSON (Steam games only), AreWeAntiCheatYet's games.json, and the Lutris games API (which indicates a community install recipe exists, not a compatibility rating). None of these cover business software. The honest design is a hand-curated internal compatibility table plus manual AppDB lookups during scoping.

Offering Winboat/WinApps to a school with 2012 laptops is not honest and should be dropped from the pitch. Three independent reasons: (1) it needs a Windows Pro/Enterprise license per device that the customer must buy, on top of the Linux migration; (2) the shipped WinApps compose allocates 4 GB RAM + 4 cores + 64 GB disk to the VM alone, and WinBoat's floor is 4 GB RAM / 2 threads / 32 GB free — a 2012-era laptop with 4 GB total cannot run the host desktop and a Windows 11 VM; (3) WinBoat is self-described BETA at v0.8.0 with no GPU acceleration and no Flatpak, so it does not fit an atomic/bootc host without layering Docker. If a customer genuinely needs Office or Adobe, the honest answer is a cloud/web version, a keep-one-Windows-machine plan, or not migrating that user — not a VM on a 14-year-old laptop.

We cannot claim Microsoft Office or Adobe support at any tier. AppDB (read directly, 2026-09-20): Office 365 Business = Garbage, Office 2021 Pro Plus = Garbage, Office 365 ProPlus = Garbage; every Photoshop CC release 2019-2024 = Silver, which upstream defines as "has some problems for which there are no workarounds", on tiny sample sizes and stale Wine versions, with no entry at all for 2025/2026. Search snippets also indicate CodeWeavers dropped Office 365 from CrossOver support in June 2026 (I could not read the page — codeweavers.com returns 403 behind Cloudflare — so treat that specific claim as unconfirmed). If our spec forbids claiming an app migrates when it doesn't, Office and Adobe must be on the explicit 'does not migrate' list, not in a caveat footnote.
